News.title: Boat capsizes in major New York harbour killing mother and baby as man arrested
News.content:
Boat capsizes in major New York harbour killing mother and baby as man arrested

Police divers located the 27-year-old woman and five-month-old girl in the water following a crash on Saturday night which saw passengers hurled from a 22-foot Bayliner speedboat into New York Harbour

View Image (Image: Bianca Otero/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Cops have arrested a man after a mother and her baby were killed in a boat accident in New York Harbour.

‌



The operator of the 22-foot Bayliner speedboat is facing criminal charges, the US coast guard said, after the vessel overturned at around 10.25pm on Saturday.

‌



The crash, which occurred close to Liberty Island, home to the Statue of Liberty, saw more than a dozen people hurled into the water.

‌



Twelve people were rescued from the waves before police arrived, and police divers later located the 27-year-old woman and five-month-old girl in the water.

Both were taken to hospital where they were tragically pronounced dead. According to the coast guard, the others were in a stable condition.

“We are deeply saddened by the tragic loss of life last night, and our thoughts are with the victims’ family and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time,” Captain Doreen McCarthy, the coast guard sector New York commander, said.

‌



“We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessels who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water.”

Cops have confirmed that Manuel Hernandez, 46, of New York, has now been charged with 13 counts of reckless endangerment in connection with the crash.

The victims’ identities have not been released pending notification of family, police said on today.

Article continues below

Coast guard investigators were working with police to investigate and were committed to holding lawbreakers accountable, Ms McCarthy said.

Authorities were investigating whether the vessel was an illegal charter, the service added.

According to the coast guard, an illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that lacks coast guard credentials, safety equipment and inspection certificates.

News.title: UK drought warnings explained as Brits could face emergency measures not used in 50 years
News.content:
UK drought warnings explained as Brits could face emergency measures not used in 50 years

Britain's contingency plans for severe drought would see standpipes set up in the street and mains water cut off at certain times of day - a state of emergency last seen in the summer of 1976

View 4 Images Residents in the worst-hit areas were forced to use standpipes (Image: Mirrorpix)

Households could face having their mains water cut off and be forced to use standpipes in the street under Britain's emergency drought plans.

Half of England is currently in an official state of drought, with much of the rest of the country classed as experiencing 'severe dry weather'. More than 20 million people in the UK are meanwhile living in an areas covered hosepipe bans - with forecasters warning that yet another heatwave is on the way this week.

But we're not yet at the highest 'red' level of warning, severe drought, which was last activated in the famous summer of 1976. Memorable scenes saw people relying on standpipes for all of their water, strict water rationing introduced, and taps running dry for much of the day.

‌



View 4 Images The last time a severe drought warning was issued - the famous summer of 1976 (Image: Getty Images)

England transformed into barren Western-like frontier as dramatic photos capture horror extent of drought READ MORE :

British food items at risk due to extreme drought - and what shortages could mean for you READ MORE :

How does Britain's drought warning system work?

The Environment Agency uses four levels of drought warning to communicate levels of risk to the public, which are:

Prolonged dry weather: Water levels are falling, and the public is encouraged to limit water use before official restrictions are needed.

Water levels are falling, and the public is encouraged to limit water use before official restrictions are needed. Drought: There is a shortage of water affecting water supplies, farming, and wildlife. Water companies implement temporary use (hosepipe bans) for households, while environmental teams may also intervene to rescue distressed wildlife, or move water locally to safeguard habitats.

There is a shortage of water affecting water supplies, farming, and wildlife. Water companies implement temporary use (hosepipe bans) for households, while environmental teams may also intervene to rescue distressed wildlife, or move water locally to safeguard habitats. Severe drought: Emergency infrastructure and contingency plans are implemented. Authorities are given the power shut off mains water and to implement 'rota cuts', which sees water turned on and off at different times of the day to manage supply. Communal street standpipes or mobile water tanks may be introduced, forcing residents to queue and carry their daily water rations back to their homes.

Emergency infrastructure and contingency plans are implemented. Authorities are given the power shut off mains water and to implement 'rota cuts', which sees water turned on and off at different times of the day to manage supply. Communal street standpipes or mobile water tanks may be introduced, forcing residents to queue and carry their daily water rations back to their homes. Recovery from drought: Issued after significant rainfall, this sees water restrictions and monitoring continue until reservoirs have fully replenished to safe levels.

View 4 Images Residents of Bideford, Devon using standpipes during the historic severe drought 50 years ago (Image: Popperfoto/Getty Images)

‌



What happens when a severe drought warning is issued?

Severe droughts are the point at which a drought truly becomes a national emergency - and they are rare. The government was last forced to raise the warning to this level in 1976, when an extraordinarily dry summer came at the end of 16 months of below average rainfall.

Along with the disruption to household water supplies, this measure also allows water companies to take more water from rivers and underground aquifers than usual, or reduce the amount they are legally required to release back into rivers from reservoirs. During the historic 1976 severe drought, the crisis became so severe that Prime Minister Harold Wilson appointed a Minister for Drought, Denis Howell, and launched massive public information campaigns urging people to share baths and place bricks in their toilet cisterns to save water.

View 4 Images Hanningfield Reservoir in Essex is one of many in Britain where water levels are currently low (Image: NEIL HALL/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



In some of the worst-hit areas, such southwest England, North Wales and Yorkshire, residents relied entirely on street standpipes for their water supply for several weeks as reservoirs dropped to unprecedented levels.

Should we expect a severe drought warning this summer?

The Environment Agency has not indicated that it is expecting to issue a warning for severe drought, with the most affected areas currently under a drought warning. Meteorologists have observed that unlike previous droughts in the UK, which typically follow several months of low rainfall, this summer has had the hallmarks of a 'flash drought' - where dry weather comes suddenly, and to a more extreme extent.

July was the driest month in southern England since records began nearly 200 years ago.

News.title: Anti-immigration protesters gather at former RAF base after Thetford unrest
News.content:
Anti-immigration protesters gather at former RAF base after Thetford unrest

Some of those who took part in violent anti-migrant protests in the town this week have attended the Sunday protest outside Barnham Camp in Suffolk amid plans it could house migrants

View 2 Images People take part in a protest outside RAF Barnham in Thetford, Norfolk which could be used to house asylum seekers. (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

Anti-immigration protestors have gathered outside a former RAF base near Thetford where violence erupted earlier this week.

‌



The Home Office announced in June that it was considering using Barnham Camp in Suffolk to accommodate people seeking asylum, sparking a series of regular protests at the site.

‌



Campaigners have gathered again today (Sunday) with Union and St George’s cross flags as some demonstrators held placards which read “Barnham says no. Protect our community”.

‌



Tensions flared in Thetford, Norfolk, earlier in the week, with one male police officer struck with a rock, while a female officer was bitten and another was spat at, police said.

Police in Norfolk said officers were “subjected to significant aggression” on Wednesday night amid three nights of unrest in the market town.

The force said on Saturday that Friday night in Thetford had been “largely peaceful”, although three people were arrested and a window was smashed.

‌



View 2 Images The Home Office announced in June that it was considering using Barnham Camp to accommodate people seeking asylum (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

Some of those who protested in the town this week included participants in the regular protests outside the former military site, the Guardian reported.

Norfolk Police were once again out to oversee anti-immigration demonstrators today at the RAF base protest. Some of those who protested in the town this week included participants in the regular protests outside the former military site, the Guardian reported.

‌



Officers said they attended to “support the lawful right to protest while helping to ensure the safety of everyone involved and the wider public”.

A Suffolk Constabulary spokesperson added: “Policing protests requires us to balance the right of individuals to peacefully express their views with our responsibility to protect local communities, including protesters, residents and road-users.

“Our policing response will continue to be kept under review, informed by the latest available information and ongoing assessments of any potential risks to public safety.

‌



“Previous protests at Ministry of Defence (MoD) Barnham have been peaceful, and we would like to thank all those involved for expressing their views in a lawful and respectful manner. We are confident that this positive approach will continue.”

The camp would accommodate men aged between 18 and 65 who have applied for asylum, according to Home Office plans which have yet to be approved.

No asylum seekers are yet housed at the site, which Suffolk Constabulary said is a training site for the Norfolk and Suffolk forces.

Article continues below

Police said some vehicles, such as buses seen on site, were used for training purposes and people on site include police, MoD employees and security staff.

News.title: Several injured in shooting in Denmark as police hunt gunmen
News.content:
Several injured in shooting in Denmark as police hunt gunmen

Police are still hunting for the attckers after several people were injured in a shooting incident in the town of Holbaek in eastern Denmark

View Image Danish police have responded to the incident (file photo) (Image: Henning Bagger/Ritzau Scanpix Fo)

Several people have been injured in a town centre shooting, as police hunt for the suspected gunmen.

‌



The attack took place in the Danish town of Holbæk, local police have said, with several people struck by gunfire. Police received the report around 3:45 pm local time (2:45pm UK time).

‌



There is no information about the condition or number of people wounded, according to local media. Nobody has yet been arrested in connection with the incident.

‌



Pictures from the scene show that the police have cordoned off a large area after the shooting. There are also police dogs at the crime scene.

According to preliminary police information, they drove from the Agervang neighbourhood, where the shooting took place, in a white car, local news reports.

Article continues below

Danish police have described the incident as a "settling of scores". In a statement on X the force said: "Police are currently present at several locations in Holbæk following a shooting where several people have been hit. It is the police's assumption that this is a settling of scores in the criminal environment."

They added: "Police received a report of the shooting around 3:45 p.m. It occurred in the Agervang residential area."

News.title: Andy Burnham mulls Railcard changes in plan to cut high train ticket prices
News.content:
Andy Burnham mulls Railcard changes in plan to cut high train ticket prices

EXCLUSIVE: New Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering extending access to railcards as part of early discussions on how to cut train ticket prices, The Mirror understands

View 2 Images The Prime Minister has said cutting rail fares is in his 'sights' (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Andy Burnham is considering extending access to railcards as part of early discussions on how to cut train ticket prices, The Mirror understands.

‌



The Prime Minister has said cutting rail fares is in his “sights”, with some prices “outrageously” high at the moment.

‌



In a signal of intent last week, he announced plans to extend the 16-17 Saver Railcard so youngsters can access it up until the day before their 19th birthday, instead of it expiring when they turn 18. The change will come into force on August 17, benefitting thousands of students with 50% off rail tickets.

‌



Government sources said discussions are taking place on extending other railcards, with talks at a “very early stage”. Officials are looking at a range of options around how to tackle the high cost of prices that go further than the rail freeze introduced this year, the Mirror has been told.

Two influential left-wing think tanks are now urging Mr Burnham to expand the network south east railcard into a national railcard.

Andy Burnham says more cost of living help on its way as struggling families in his sights READ MORE :

View 2 Images In a signal of intent last week, Andy Burnham announced plans to extend the 16-17 Saver Railcard (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



The railcard, which costs £35 a year, gives train users a third off most rail fares for journeys in London and the south east. Anyone 16 years and above can buy one.

Elsewhere in the country, railcards exist for particular age groups including adults aged up to 30 or those over 60, or groups including disabled people or veterans, but there is not a universal discount card. It means adults aged 31 to 59 are unable to access this discount outside the south east.

Zoë Billingham, director of IPPR North, who informally advised Mr Burnham on an unpaid sabbatical this summer, said it is not “coherent” that the universal railcard only exists in one part of the country.

‌



She told The Mirror: “I do think there would be a sensible question at this stage that says, well, given the kind of unfairness from the passengers' perspective, from the public's perspective of just having a network railcard that covers the south east, why shouldn't that be something that's offered more broadly?

“So I would be very supportive of the government looking at that for the country as a whole. Fundamentally, transport is about jobs, it's about connecting people socially.

“But it also helps the government with its climate goals, getting people off cars and onto more green modes of transport. So it ticks a lot of boxes and so I'd be really supportive of the government moving in that direction.”

‌



Ms Billingham added that as the network railcard is already an established scheme, an extension of it could be “mobilised quickly”. This compares to longer term structural fare reforms that are likely to be looked at as part of rail nationalisation under Great British Railways.

Hannah Peaton, deputy chief executive at the New Economics Foundation (NEF), echoed that an extension of the southeast railcard is an “obvious opportunity” to make the system more equal across the country.

She told The Mirror: “If you take an off-peak, non-advanced journey from London to Milton Keynes, it costs around £23/24, and that's similar to the cost of a trip from Manchester to Leeds.

‌



“But for no real reason, the Milton Keynes trip is eligible for the one third discount, and the Manchester/Leeds one isn't. Which, if you take that in the context of Burnham being very specific that he really wants to ensure equivalent living standards in all parts of the UK, it just feels like an obvious opportunity to equalise it.”

NEF, which last month produced a report looking at bus and rail fares, estimates the policy would generate £425million in consumer savings.

Its modelling suggests it would have a net cost of £270m in the first year, falling to £120m over the long-term, however it said new ticket sales and card sales would to a large extent offset the costs of the scheme.

‌



Ms Peaton added: “I suppose the other really exciting thing about the policy is it effectively pays for itself…So it feels like a no-brainer. It's a chance to take an existing benefit that, for no real reason, only applies to the south east.”

In an interview with The Mirror earlier this month, Mr Burnham said the cost of living is at the top of his priorities list. "I think rail fares are too high, outrageously so in some instances,” he added. “So that's something that's in my sights.”

Mr Burnham used his first days in Downing Street to roll out a rapid-fire list of cost of living announcements. VAT will be slashed from electricity bills from October, bus fares will be capped at £2 and pubs, social clubs and live music venues will get a 20% cut to business rates from April.

Article continues below

At last year’s Budget, former Chancellor Rachel Reeves announced a freeze on rail fares for the first time in 30 years, though prices of tickets still remain high.

Announcing the 16-17 Saver Railcard extension last week, Rail Minister Lord Peter Hendy said: "This kind of common-sense change is exactly what passengers should expect from the railway.”

News.title: 'I want to change my name but I'm worried my choice will stop me getting a job'
News.content:
'I want to change my name but I'm worried my choice will stop me getting a job'

A woman has sought advice on changing her first name to something 'memorable' after admitting employers may find her decision 'ridiculous' due to her existing surname

View Image A woman fears her name change will be deemed 'ridiculous' (stock) (Image: Viktoriya Skorikova/Moment via Getty Images)

A woman who is considering legally changing her first name to one she has used for three years has expressed concerns that doing so will affect her job prospects - due to her surname. Taking to Reddit, she sought advice over fears her prospective new name would be deemed "ridiculous" by others.

‌



"I have used Summer socially for about three years and am considering making it my legal first name," she began in a post. "The problem is that my surname is Winter."

‌



The woman said she initially thought putting the two together would be "funny in a harmless way" - but now she's having second thoughts. "Now that I am imagining it on job applications, medical forms, and professional email signatures, I am less certain," she confessed. "I do not want every introduction to begin with a joke about the seasons."

‌



She went on to muse: " Is Summer Winter memorable or just ridiculous?" She added Summer isn't her only option, however.

"Changing my surname is not something I want to do," she said. "My other possible first names are Simone and Mara, but neither feels as natural as Summer."

‌



She closed her post in the Names subreddit with a plea, writing: "Would Summer Winter sound intentionally theatrical or fictional to you? Does the repetition make it unusable in a professional setting, or is it simply a name people would remember for five seconds and then accept? Please be direct. My friends definitely are not."

The verdict was overwhelming. "Last name being Winter is one of the very few situations where you absolutely should not use Summer," one Reddit user shared. A second person agreed: "I'd make a joke every time I'd see you, not just the first meeting."

A third commented: "Sorry, hard pass. It's a beautiful name, and Winter is a cool last name, but together it sounds like a sitcom or a kid's show character. I'm a big fan of Mara Winter. Simone has a nicer flow."

‌



While a fourth Reddit user declared: "Pretty silly. I know it shouldn't matter, but society is what it is. If you keep that name, it's going to be hard for people to take you seriously as an intelligent person."

What are the rules around changing your name?

According to the government, you can change any part of your name, add or remove names or hyphens, or change the spelling.

Your new name must:

Article continues below

be pronounceable

not include symbols, numbers or punctuation (unless it’s a hyphenated name or part of an established name like O’Hara)

not be offensive or against the public interest (for example, adding Ltd to the end of the name)

News.title: 'I worked for Royal Family and had to make bizarre check in case Princess Anne was jailed'
News.content:
'I worked for Royal Family and had to make bizarre check in case Princess Anne was jailed'

A former royal aide has revealed the unusual preparations that were made before Princess Anne faced court over an incident involving one of her dogs

View 3 Images The Princess Royal (Image: PA)

A former royal aide has revealed an extraordinary security precaution that had to be taken before Princess Anne appeared in court.

‌



Ailsa Anderson, who served as Press Secretary to Queen Elizabeth II, was speaking to The Sun’s Royal Exclusive host Matt Wilkinson and royal journalist Phil Dampier when she recalled the remarkable preparations surrounding the case.

‌



It came after Princess Anne pleaded guilty to an offence involving one of her dogs — but behind the scenes, royal officials had to prepare for an outcome nobody wanted to see.

‌



Ailsa explained that she had been present at Slough Magistrates’ Court in 2002, where the Princess Royal faced the charge after her English bull terrier, known as Dotty, attacked two children.

The former royal staff member said: “I was there in Slough Magistrates’ Court. She lost control of her dogs. She pleaded guilty.”

But the conversation then took an unexpected turn.

‌



View 3 Images Princess Anne (Image: 2026 Getty Images)

“Yeah. Again, we had to recce the courts beforehand and look at the jails downstairs just in case they pushed her down.”

Phil initially remembered the incident as involving a cyclist, before Anderson clarified: “No, it was children. It was a child in Windsor Great Park.”

‌



Matt then asked: “Sorry, sorry. You had to check the cells?”

Ailsa replied: “Yes, just in case she was sent down.” Matt then asked: “That could have happened?” before Ailsa confirmed: “We checked the cells.”

The extraordinary preparations were carried out for security reasons, with Ailsa explaining that officials needed to know what was inside the cells and who might be there.

‌



“There were a few,” she said when asked whether there were criminals downstairs.

Asked whether the cells were suitable for a member of the royal family, she replied: “They were basic, Matt. They were basic. Not quite what she was used to, right? But she didn’t have to go to any of these cells.”

Princess Anne ultimately avoided prison, receiving a £500 fine and being ordered to pay £500 compensation. She was also ordered to pay £148 in court costs, while Dotty had to be kept on a lead in public and undergo training.

‌



View 3 Images Princess Anne (Image: WireImage)

The case was particularly significant as it marked the first time a senior member of the Royal Family had been convicted of a criminal offence. No other senior royal had attended court for around a century.

The case against Anne’s husband, Commodore Tim Laurence, was dropped shortly after the hearing began.

‌



The Princess Royal’s punishment was criticised by members of the victims’ families, who were angry that Dotty was not ordered to be put down.

District Judge Penelope Hewitt said the couple were experienced dog owners, but warned that another incident could result in the animal being destroyed.

Despite the preparations made in case Anne was sent to prison, Anderson confirmed the Princess never actually saw the cells herself.

Article continues below

Matt then asked: “Did she go to look at them herself?”

“No. No,” Ailsa replied.

News.title: How weight-loss medication is changing relationships with alcohol
News.content:
There is a growing body of research into the link between weight-loss drugs and alcohol consumption.

The drugs, with brands including Wegovy, Mounjaro and Ozempic, contain semaglutide or tirzepatide, which mimic a natural hormone called GLP-1. This suppresses appetite and keeps people feeling fuller for longer, helping them to lose weight.

Early research suggests that because these drugs affect the reward response in the brain, they can reduce cravings for substances including alcohol and nicotine, says Dr Christian Hendershot of the University of South Carolina.

He published a small-scale study, external in 2025 in which participants with alcohol use disorder craved alcohol less while taking Ozempic. Alcohol use disorder, sometimes referred to as alcoholism, is described by the NHS as drinking in a way that is harmful.

A study, external from the University of Colorado Anschutz published last week also suggested that GLP-1 medications in pill form led to fewer days of heavy drinking in people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder.

People taking the drugs told BBC News that alcohol had affected them in different ways: some said their cravings for it had gone, drinking had made them feel nauseous or uncomfortably full, or they had got drunk more quickly. Others said they had not noticed any effect on their relationship with alcohol.

Before she started taking Wegovy, Lisa says she drank between six and eight bottles of wine a week with friends. But she had sometimes worried about whether this was too much and whether it could damage her health.

NHS guidance, external is that people should not drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, which is about six medium glasses of wine or six pints. Drinking too much in the long term can lead to liver damage, high blood pressure and increased risk of cancer.

Lisa says that since starting on the medication she has more than halved her consumption. At a recent day festival, she drank three glasses of wine over the course of nine hours. Previously, she would have had two bottles plus a couple of vodka mixers, she says.

Alcohol has always been a big part of her social life and when she stopped drinking for a few weeks in the late 2010s, she realised friends had stopped inviting her to social events. It led her to start drinking again.

This time round, Lisa says that she still looks forward to drinking wine, but after having a couple of glasses she simply cannot stomach any more.

"I still feel involved in things because I'm still drinking but drinking a lot less," Lisa says.

For years, Warren Thomas, 45, from Colchester, had enjoyed an occasional beer with his family after work, as well as one or two heavy drinking sessions with his friends each month.

But when he spoke to his friends on weight-loss medication about his plans to start taking Mounjaro, they warned him that it could affect how much he drank.

Warren says he noticed the effect within 24 hours of his first dose in mid-June. "I just don't want to drink," he says. "I've just got no appetite for it."

When he went out for his friend's birthday last month, he felt "light-headed and a little bit giddy" after two beers, he says.

"My tolerance level to drinking is now zero," he says.

There is no formal advice in the British National Formulary, a guide to dispensing medicine used by doctors and pharmacists, about whether people on weight-loss drugs should stop drinking alcohol, says Prof Russell Hearn, a GP and professor of medicine at King's College London.

But he gives careful advice to his patients. "Alcohol has a lot of calories in it and if your goal is to lose weight, drinking less will definitely help you with that alongside changing your diet while you're on a GLP-1," he says.

For people like Lisa and Warren, drinking less alcohol has been a happy bonus. But recent graduate Faye Goodwin, 20, feels that it has hampered her social life.

When Faye drinks she says she gets nauseous very quickly and sometimes throws up or gets bad acid reflux.

Faye, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice, has been taking Mounjaro since she was 18 and does not really know what it is like to drink alcohol without the impact of weight-loss medication. But she says she once took a month off the jabs and was able to drink without experiencing any nausea.

News.title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
News.content:
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost Â£150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than Â£85,000.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent Â£50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further Â£35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.

The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.

Banksy, who emerged from Bristol's graffiti scene in the 1990s and became one of the world's most famous street artists, is known for murals and installations that often appear overnight and attract large crowds.

The latest costs relate to a mural depicting a judge in a wig battering a protester with his gavel, which appeared on the Royal Courts of Justice in London on 8 September 2025.

Banksy claimed the image as his own work, by posting it on his website and Instagram account.

News.title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
News.content:
After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?

A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising.

But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer.

The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors.

In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a â¬150,000 (Â£128,000) fine, if convicted.

Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Ãtape forest in the Vosges region.

"Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est RÃ©publicain, the newspaper that reported the story.

Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts.

"I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction.

The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame.

The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues.

But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances.

"The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying.

News.title: Man arrested after boat capsizes near Statue of Liberty killing woman and infant
News.content:
The operator of a boat that overturned near the Statue of Liberty, killing a woman and a baby, has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment, New York police said.

Officials said a large search and rescue operation was launched after the incident near New York Harbour on Saturday night.

A nearby vessel rescued 12 people from the water before police arrived, the US Coast Guard (USCG) said.

New York police divers later found a 27-year-old woman and a five-month-old girl, who were transported to a nearby hospital where they later died.

The names of passengers and the specific cause of the incident have not been released.

Around 22:25 local time (03:25 BST), police received a 911 call reporting an overturned boat in the waters near Liberty Island, which houses the iconic statue.

The rescue involved two Coast Guard boats, four fire department boats, two police boats and a police helicopter, the USCG said. The survivors of the incident are all reported to be in stable condition, the agency added.

The investigation into the incident is ongoing, officials said. The boat's operator, a 46-year-old Manhattan resident, faces 13 counts of reckless endangerment, officials said.

Coast Guard investigators are also determining whether the boat was illegally chartered. An illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that does not have required credentials, safety equipment, and certificate of inspection.

"We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessel who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water," said Capt Doreen McCarthy of the USCG.

News.title: More areas of UK likely to move into drought as fifth heatwave builds
News.content:
As the hot and dry weather continues for much of the UK, drought status could be declared in additional parts of England this week.

The Environment Agency (EA) has suggested that "several areas" of England could enter drought status as "public water supplies remain under increasing pressure with continued dry weather and high demand".

For the seventh consecutive week, less than 10mm of rain fell across the country, with east and south-east England seeing less than 1mm of rain, according to data from the agency's latest drought summary.

More than half of England and the whole of Wales are already under drought conditions.

Reservoir levels have continued to fall, with almost all across England below normal and five classed as 'exceptionally low', according to the EA.

Wisley in Surrey has gone more than 50 days without a drop of rain. Southern England is approaching two months without any notable rainfall.

Customers of South West Water were the latest to see a hosepipe ban introduced on Saturday.

There are now more than 20 million people in the UK living in an area where prolonged dry weather combined with heatwaves and high demand for water has led to restrictions on usage.

Update: A previous version of this story said that the UK had recorded 35 days of temperatures exceeding 30C, breaking the previous record. As of 9 August, the UK has equalled the 1995 record, with 34 days of temperatures exceeding 30C.

News.title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
News.content:
"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.

Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.

Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.

Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland â in the south-western corner of Australia â is one of the few places they remain.

As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.

Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.

This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.

Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.

News.title: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock
News.content:
"I can't zip this! Mummm?"

This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.

The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.

She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood.

"She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me.

"It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off."

"Iâm still in shock,â she adds. âThe thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."

The interaction went viral, external with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.

While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" â where stars match outfits to a film's themes â Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.

Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun.

"Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.â

News.title: Why eclipse chasers are crossing continents for solar spectacle: 'It's like the World Cup'
News.content:
On Wednesday, parts of Europe will be plunged into daytime darkness as the moon passes in front of the sun, temporarily blocking its light and casting a shadow across the continent.

For many of us, it will be a once-in-a-lifetime experience. But for some, following eclipses has become something of an addiction.

Armed with two high-spec cameras, a specialist telescope and a drone, Mark Griffiths has spent two days driving from Cheshire to Galicia - one of the best places to view the eclipse - to record the event.

It's a hobby that started six years ago, when he went to Shetland to see the northern lights - though the weather was so dreary he "didn't see anything".

But it didn't put him off and he soon found he couldn't stop. He loved the thrill of witnessing and capturing the sky's most spectacular events.

News.title: Andy Burnham to embark on cost of living tour through the UK
News.content:
The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Downing Street says.

No 10 says Andy Burnham's plans are to "give people some room to breathe". He will also focus on ways of "improving high streets" as he embarks on a tour of the UK.

But the government is facing continued pressure over its early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales â with criticism of the fact that two of PC Andrew Harper's killers will be eligible from next year.

Burnham is also likely to face pressure for more action on the cost of living â although significant interventions are unlikely before October's Budget.

Even then, Chancellor John Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

The prime minister has been on holiday this week, but Downing Street said he would be in "listening mode" in the coming days as he tours the UK's nations and regions and works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

A spokesman for the prime minister said: "He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles â like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off â must be accepted as part of life.

"He doesn't think that's right. That's why he's going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe."

The spokesman added: "He's also going to be kicking off his summer tour around the country, getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are.

"The prime minister is going to be in listening mode to help inform his 10-year plan to bring back hope and make Britain better off."

There are, though, likely to be continued questions about the forthcoming early release scheme, due to start in October.

One of Burnham's first acts in Downing Street was to order a review which limited the range of people who would be eligible.

But those convicted of manslaughter will still qualify for the scheme â including two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.

The prime minister has faced calls from PC Harper's family, former senior police officers and opposition politicians for them to be denied early release.

But he has said he cannot go any further without risking prison capacity. Downing Street said on Saturday night that position remained unchanged, despite reports the prime minister could revisit the case.

News.title: Family 'devastated' as hit-and-run driver who killed boy, 13, to have early prison release
News.content:
The family of a 13-year-old boy killed in a hit-and-run say they are "devastated" after being told the driver who caused his death has had his sentence reduced.

Kaylan Hippsley died three days after being struck by a car driven by Harley Whiteman on Brecon Road in Hirwaun, Rhondda Cynon Taf, on 29 February 2024.

Whiteman was originally sentenced to six years and nine months in prison and banned from driving for eight years and four months but, after Kaylan's family appealed, High Court judges increased the sentence to nine years.

Now, the family has been told Whiteman can be released under licence as early as this autumn as part of the UK government's Sentencing Act early release scheme.

News.title: Holiday 'completely overshadowed' by loss of airport luggage
News.content:
Travellers have described struggling to enjoy their holidays, days after hundreds of people flying out of Birmingham Airport were left without their luggage.

While it seems the issues that first emerged on Friday are yet to be remedied completely, the airport said the "vast majority" of baggage was now travelling as planned with passengers, and it was working to reunite others with their luggage.

Louise Fenton said she and her family had had no communication from the airline, holiday company or the airport after their luggage failed to arrive in Gran Canaria on Friday.

She is travelling with three teenagers, and said her daughter, who is autistic, had "struggled enormously" with replacement clothes, and had "barely slept because she is unable to tolerate the alternatives".

"We are staying in a tourist area where the shops are predominantly beach shops, with very limited clothing options, particularly for someone with sensory sensitivities," the mum explained.

"We still have no luggage and, no meaningful information about where it is."

She added the situation had "completely overshadowed" the holiday.

"We have worked hard and saved for this holiday, and we simply don't deserve to have the entire experience taken over by something that isn't our fault."

Speaking to the BBC on Friday and Saturday, travellers variously described the situation as "absolute chaos" and "carnage".

Other flights affected include ones to Turkey, Cyprus, Glasgow and Rome, covering a number of airlines.

News.title: Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
News.content:
EastEnders star Kellie Bright is to leave the soap after playing one of its key characters, Linda Carter, for 13 years.

She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick, portrayed by Danny Dyer, when they became the new owners of the Queen Vic pub.

Carter's matriarch character has been central to major storylines including plots about murder, sexual assault and alcoholism.

Bright said she made the "tough decision" to leave more than a year ago but "happily" agreed to stay on to be part of an "exciting storyline".

The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her on-screen exit, which is said to be a "while away" yet.

Executive producer Ben Wadey described the actor as being "the beating heart of EastEnders" and said she had become "a classic EastEnders icon".

Viewers have seen the much-loved character at the heart of many emotional storylines including in 2014 when she was raped by her brother-in-law Dean Wicks.

More than 7 million people watched the episode which prompted dozens of complaints. The sexual assault led to long-running story arc about family conflict and trauma.

News.title: Rare turtle to be sent back home in 5,000-mile 'incredibly emotional' trip
News.content:
It has taken almost two years to plan, including building a special temperature-controlled crate for him, and co-ordinating complex paperwork across two countries.

Rhossi normally lives in the sea, but has to travel out of the water â first by helicopter from Anglesey to London, then by cargo flight to Houston, Texas, USA.

It means the journey needs to be completed as quickly as possible, and staff have to be constantly on hand to make sure he does not dry out or dehydrate.

Davidson said: "We have to make sure that the shell is really well lubricated, so we spread Vaseline all over to stop it drying out and flaking off.

"The same for the skin â it's really delicate â and especially the eyes, which both have to be lubricated before he goes into the crate and again just before takeoff, or he will start to peel like someone getting sunburned.

"But I have had to go to the checkout in a chemist's with about eight tubes of KY Jelly and three tubs of Vaseline and explain what's happening when I get strange looks."

News.title: Hot weather reveals hidden history across the South
News.content:
As the south of England continues to enjoy an unusually warm and dry summer, parch marks on lawns across the region have revealed the hidden histories of their location.

Among the sites which have seen the outlines of historic installations exposed by the hot weather are Portchester Castle and Blenheim Palace.

At Blenheim, the footprint of an 18th century garden - which had once stretched across the width of the entire palace - has revealed itself on a lawn.

Andy Mills, the Unesco World Heritage Site's head gardener, told the BBC it was "absolutely magical" to see the outlines of the historic parterre - 260 years after it was demolished.

Mills explained that the original parterre - which is a French word meaning 'on the ground' - had been constructed in 1705, and would have "cost an absolute fortune to install".

"It was a very large extravagant thing to do, but it was a way of showing your wealth and importance and that sort of thing," he said.

News.title: Attempted murder arrest after three hit by car
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and dangerous driving after three pedestrians were hit by a car following reports of a disturbance.

The incident happened on Stokes Croft in Bristol at about 06:30 BST, according to Avon and Somerset Police.

A spokesperson for the force said one of the pedestrians was taken to hospital, but their injuries were not considered to be life-changing or life-threatening. The two others were not seriously injured.

A man police believe to be the car's driver was treated for facial injuries after his arrest.

Thomas Street, Hepburn Road, Stokes Croft and City Road are all closed while police make enquiries, with more officers than usual in the area as investigations continue.

The Best Off Licence in Stokes Croft was also damaged in the incident.

Bristol Supt Matt Ebbs said: "We would like to assure the public we do not believe there to be any wider threat.

"Anybody with concerns is welcome to speak to officers on the ground, but we would also appeal to anybody with CCTV, dashcam or mobile phone footage which may assist our enquiries to contact us."

News.title: Stray cats showing up at raves, gigs and pubs now have own merchandise
News.content:
Celebs pulling in punters with a club appearance is nothing new. But did they ever have so much fur?

At venues in Coventry at least, the glitterati wear whiskers these days.

It began when two stray cats made city venues their home, becoming social media stars thanks to the incongruous sights of tail and turntable, pint and paw.

While one shows up at gigs and rave nights, the other is a bit more pub than dub. But each now has his own range of merch... and visitors flock for a glimpse of these meeow-vers and shakers.

Murphy was first spotted living beneath a bush before wandering into the car park of The Old Windmill pub in the city centre, "rake thin" and in need of care.

Now a permanent resident, he has become a firm favourite with customers.

"We've had people who've never been in the pub before, but have seen him on social media," said the venue's Peter Dunkley. "They come in and the first question is 'where's Murphy'?"

Across town, Fargo is a well-known figure at Fargo Village, the creative hub after which he is named.

Regularly spotted around the site's shops and bars, he too has become an attraction in his own right, mixing among ravers and drinkers.

Fargo Village staff have set up an Instagram account in an effort to track down his owner, and it has attracted a loyal following of fans eager to keep up with his daily adventures.

News.title: Man charged after mother and infant killed as boat capsizes in New York Harbor
News.content:

The operator of a boat that capsized in New York Harbor, killing a mother and her five-month-old daughter, is facing criminal charges as authorities investigate whether the vessel was being used as an illegal charter, the U.S. Coast Guard said Sunday.

The 22-foot Bayliner speedboat overturned at about 10:25 p.m. Saturday near Liberty Island, where the Statue of Liberty is located, according to the Coast Guard.

According to the Coast Guard, NYPD divers, New York Fire Department first responders, two Coast Guard vessels and an NYPD helicopter responded to a report of “persons on board going into the water.”

Twelve people were rescued from the water before police arrived. Police divers later found the 27-year-old woman and her infant daughter in the water. Both were taken to NYU Langone Brooklyn, where they were pronounced dead. The remaining passengers were in stable condition, the Coast Guard said.

Manuel Hernandez, 46, of New York, has been charged with 13 counts of reckless endangerment ( Ryan Hiscott/Getty Images )

“We are deeply saddened by the tragic loss of life last night, and our thoughts are with the victims’ family and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time,” said Captain Doreen McCarthy, commander of Coast Guard Sector New York. “We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessel who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water."

Manuel Hernandez, 46, of New York, has been charged with 13 counts of reckless endangerment, police said. Hernandez was arrested by the NYPD at around 2:30 a.m. Sunday, roughly four hours after his boat capsized. No phone number for him could be found Sunday, and the case has not yet been entered into online court records.

An illegal charter is a passenger-for-hire vessel operating without the required U.S. Coast Guard credentials, safety equipment or certificate of inspection. Such vessels may not meet the safety standards required of legal charter operations, potentially putting paying passengers at greater risk.

The victims' identities have not been released pending notification of family, police said Sunday.

The Coast Guard, along with its investigative service and the NYPD, is actively investigating the circumstances and cause of the fatal vessel capsizing.

News.title: Kasper Hogh hat-trick powers Celtic to Kilmarnock thrashing without Martin O’Neill
News.content:

New Celtic striker Kasper Hogh delivered a tonic for the recuperating Martin O’Neill with a first-half hat-trick at Kilmarnock in the absence of his manager.

The Dane got off the mark in a Celtic jersey as the champions beat Killie 5-1 on the new grass pitch at Rugby Park to jump above St Mirren on goal difference at the top of the William Hill Premiership.

Shaun Maloney took charge of Celtic as O’Neill rested following an overnight hospital stay in midweek following what the club called a “small procedure”.

The 74-year-old was able to visit his players at the team hotel beforehand and they produced their highest-scoring league performance since beating Aberdeen by the same scoreline in May 2025.

open image in gallery Shaun Maloney was in charge for Celtic’s fixture at Kilmarnock (Robert Perry/PA) ( PA Wire )

Benjamin Nygren put Celtic four up just after the interval before Michael Schjonning-Larsen netted a consolation for Killie, who created a steady stream of chances in the opening stages, although they were already one down by that point. Luke McCowan finished the rout in the 75th minute.

While Maloney deputised for O’Neill, there was another important figure from Celtic’s history present in Ayrshire. North America-based former owner Fergus McCann, the man who turned around the club’s fortunes off the pitch in the mid-1990s, made a rare appearance at a Celtic game.

Celtic again started with Alistair Johnston and Arne Engels amid respective interest from Everton and West Ham, although the Canada right-back made way for Colby Donovan at half-time.

The game was over by that point and the writing was on the wall for Killie after just 70 seconds when Hogh headed home a left-wing Engels cross from close range.

Killie’s initial response was positive as the game swung from end to end. Aaron Tshibola and Tom Lowery had shots blocked with Celtic scrambling, Erik Ring knocked the ball wide from close range and both Tyreece John-Jules and Greg Kiltie had efforts saved by Viljami Sinisalo.

But Celtic were creating chances throughout. Camilo Duran, Engels and Nygren all threatened twice and Max Stryjek also made saves from Hogh and Kieran Tierney before the visitors doubled their lead in the 33rd minute.

Killie centre-back Johnly Yfeko gifted possession inside his own half and passes from Callum McGregor, Duran and Nygren quickly set up Hogh to finish first time.

The summer signing from Bodo/Glimt completed his hat-trick two minutes later as Celtic again broke quickly after winning the ball back inside their own half. Yfeko charged well out of position and nobody ever picked up Hogh before the Dane nodded Duran’s cross home from close range.

open image in gallery Kasper Hogh scored a first-half hat-trick against Kilmarnock ( PA )

Dozens of Killie fans headed for the exits 100 seconds after the interval when Nygren finished after being gifted the ball by Stryjek. They would not even have been out the stadium by the time Duran hit the crossbar.

Killie manager Neil McCann soon became involved in an argument with a supporter who had stayed behind and matters nearly deteriorated as Hogh, Tierney and Yang all came close.

Schjonning-Larsen finished off a measured passing move in the 56th minute but it proved a brief respite for the hosts.

Hogh headed off the post before substitute McCowan hooked home after a corner and Stryjek kept the score down with stops from Sebastian Tounekti, the hat-trick hero and James Forrest.

Elsewhere, three Hearts summer signings were on target as Wouter Vrancken belatedly got his reign up and running with an emphatic 4-0 win over Dundee United.

Tom Renaud, Calvin Miller and Josh McPake all marked their first league outings at Tynecastle with goals, while last season’s talisman Claudio Braga broke his duck for the campaign, as Vrancken ended a run of four consecutive defeats since taking the reins.

Former Hearts boss Derek McInnes suffered a damaging home debut as Rangers manager with a defeat to Hibernian with star striker Youssef Chermiti carried off the pitch on a stretcher.

Rangers thought they’d salvaged a point when an 85th-minute Miguel Chaiwa own goal cancelled out Josh Campbell opener, only for Callum Wright to fire home a stunning stoppage-time effort to sink the Ibrox club.

Motherwell meanwhile signed off for their Conference League third-round qualifier against HJK Helsinki with a goalless draw against Falkirk.

News.content:

To understand the 127 Yard Sale, it helps to start on a back road in rural Ohio, where a 12-foot rooster statue towers before a red barn. Alternatively, route to a two-lane stretch in Tennessee, where a vendor’s sign propped inside an open casket promises a “killer deal.”

For nearly 700 miles — stretching along Highway 127 in southern Michigan down to Lookout Mountain Parkway, Alabama — the nation’s longest yard sale winds through open farmland, mountain bluffs and small towns.

Along the four-day route, tables hold a mix of everyday attic clear-outs and true oddities.

Shoppers sift through classic roadside fare like vintage tools, mid-century furniture, milk glass and car parts, mixed with items you would be hard pressed to find anywhere else. Over the years, vendors have set up everything from Victorian wheelchairs and antique farm machinery to full-sized replica dinosaurs and even a vintage embalming table.

“Every year, people ask me, ‘What is it like?’” Josh Randall, the director of media relations for the 127 Yard Sale, told The Independent. “It’s one of those things where, until you experience it yourself, it’s very hard to put into words because it’s on such a massive scale. People think yard sale, they think the Saturday morning kind of thing. But because it’s so big, it’s like you’re going to an event. You're not just going to a yard sale.”

open image in gallery At the 127 Yard Sale, which spans Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee, Georgia and Alabama, shoppers pick through miles of roadside treasures, hunting down everything from vintage chairs and mid-century furniture to full-sized replica dinosaurs ( 127 Yard Sale )

open image in gallery Map of the 127 Yard Sale route from Addison, Michigan, to Gadsden, Alabama ( 127 Yard Sale )

The event’s origins trace back to 1987, when Mike Walker, then county executive of Fentress County in Jamestown, Tennessee, hatched a plan to lure vacationers off major interstates. The goal was to redirect tourist traffic onto two-lane back roads, giving small rural communities along Highway 127 a chance to show off their local businesses, parks and regional culture.

The local experiment quickly caught on. Neighboring communities across Kentucky, Ohio and surrounding states wanted to be part of it, eventually expanding the route into the six-state corridor it is today.

“Over the following years, Ohio was added to it, Georgia down into Alabama, and eventually the last portion that was added was into the southern portion of Michigan,” Randall said. Next year, he added, marks the sale’s 40th anniversary.

Spanning nearly 700 miles, the event is so vast that even those who run it struggle to capture its magnitude. With no single entry point or gate count to rely on, organizers estimate that participation climbs into the hundreds of thousands, driven by more than 10,000 vendors spread across all six states.

open image in gallery A roadside sign propped inside an open casket promises a ‘killer deal’ along a 700-mile stretch of rural back roads ( 127 Yard Sale )

open image in gallery A replica dinosaur at the 127 Yard Sale ( 127 Yard Sale )

Navigating the sale requires patience and a willingness to abandon strict schedules. Because traffic slows to a crawl through the heavy vendor clusters, driving Highway 127 means surrendering to the pace of the road.

“You might show up somewhere and think you're going to be there for ten minutes,” Randall said, "and the next thing you know, you're talking to a vendor and you're there for two hours.”

For Randall, that unhurried pace is precisely what gives the sale its staying power. Having traveled the entire 700-mile corridor multiple times, he sees the event as a rare reprieve from an increasingly digital world.

“Today, so much of our lives is digital — we’re on social media, we’re doing email,” he said. “Actually being in person and talking to other human beings face-to-face is becoming more of a unique thing. People spend a lot of time talking, and there’s a real community aspect to it.”

open image in gallery Beyond typical household clutter, the route features massive specialty collections, including extensive sets of vintage toy cars ( 127 Yard Sale )

open image in gallery A collection of salt-and-pepper shakers at the 127 Yard Sale ( 127 Yard Sale )

That desire to talk to actual people mirrors a broader trend in the explosion of second-hand shopping and secondhand culture. In recent years, thrifting and vintage hunting have transformed what used to be a weekend hobby into a massive secondary economy, fueled in large part by social media creators, digital resellers and content creators looking for unique pieces.

The 127 Yard Sale Facebook community alone has grown to more than 199,000 members, serving as a year-round online home base where shoppers post wish lists, vendors share photos of incoming merchandise and property owners rent out booth spaces for about $25 per day.

Yet while platforms like TikTok, Instagram and online marketplaces have introduced a younger generation to the thrill of second-hand treasure hunting, Randall notes that digital hype can only take you so far.

open image in gallery Driven by viral social media trends, a younger generation of content creators is heading to Highway 127 for old-fashioned, face-to-face dealmaking ( 127 Yard Sale )

open image in gallery Property owners along the route turn front yards and empty pastures into bustling outdoor markets charging around $25 a day per booth ( 127 Yard Sale )

The online space helps build anticipation, but it ultimately serves to feed the real-world experience.

Influencers and content creators now travel the route to document their journeys in real time, drawing viewers into a culture centered on tactile discovery — sifting through physical crates, bargaining over old tools or vintage fashion and connecting directly with the seller.

Beyond individual sellers clearing out attics, the event provides an essential economic lift to small towns along the route. One indoor antique mall in Chattanooga, Tennessee, recorded four-day sales totals during the event that eclipsed its entire previous month’s revenue.

Revenue aside, most people come for the simple joy of the drive.

“You get to experience something you wouldn't normally,” Randall said.

When Anfield had last hosted Liverpool, as Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson bade farewell and their teammates embarked on their final lap of honour, Arne Slot had remained sat in the dugout. It proved the last sighting of him in Liverpool. Some 11 weeks later, Slot’s successor was a visible presence on the edge of the technical area, Andoni Iraola’s constant clapping encouraging his players at the start of a new era. It began with echoes of the old: a 3-2 defeat to Monaco, with a lead lost at Anfield, and with a goal conceded to a set-piece, had some similarities with Slot’s unravelling, even if the stakes were lower.

Iraola may hope the parallels with last season end when the competitive football starts. As it was, Liverpool outlined why they require Ronald Araujo and how their recruitment is unfinished. They have a left-back – Robertson’s replacement is his former deputy, a returning Kostas Tsimikas making his Anfield comeback – but Salah’s old spot remains unfilled. Lewis Koumas was a locum in the place of a legend on the right flank; the Welsh winger may be destined for a fourth straight loan spell rather than a run in the team.

open image in gallery Andoni Iraola still has work to do in the transfer market, as was evident in his Anfield bow against Monaco ( PA )

His presence was an illustration that Liverpool’s business stalled after the June signing of Victor Munoz. They are yet to achieve their main objective. One ambitious target, Yan Diomande, has already eluded them. Another is out of reach as long as there is a significant difference between Liverpool’s valuation of Bradley Barcola and Paris Saint-Germain’s. There is no point in putting in a bid now when the European champions want well over £100m.

Liverpool have shown a willingness to pay such sums in the past; but their budget is limited now. Their two £100m men from 2025 struck in a way that at least offered optimism they will deliver more this season than last.

Alexander Isak only found the net twice at Anfield in his debut campaign for Liverpool; a friendly goal will not count towards his official tally but was guided in after a pass from Ryan Gravenberch. Isak and Florian Wirtz struck in the same game, which they only did once for Slot. The German got a poacher’s goal, bundling the ball over the line after Cody Gakpo’s header was blocked. If Wirtz alternated between central and wide roles under Slot, Iraola has installed him as his No 10.

open image in gallery Alexander Isak (right) and Florian Wirtz were both on target against Monaco ( Reuters )

There seems a clarity to that and a more vertical brand of football after the passiveness of Slotball irritated Anfield. Distinct differences were apparent in Iraola’s home bow. It was notable that the full-backs were often far more advanced than Gravenberch. That may suit Jeremie Frimpong and Milos Kerkez, though the latter did not start against Monaco, more than Slot’s style of football did. Yet it also gives a need for centre-backs who can defend one on one.

And, as Liverpool turned victory into defeat, they underlined why the middle of the defence has been the other focus of their recruitment drive, and why additions are necessary. Araujo is undergoing a medical before he completes his surprise loan from Barcelona. Jeremy Jacquet and Giovanni Leoni, the youngsters who arrived for a combined fee of almost £100m, are yet to play in pre-season; Joe Gomez is already injured.

Virgil van Dijk, in his first appearance since the World Cup, could be forgiven for rustiness when he tripped Aleksandr Golovin to concede a penalty the Russian converted himself. Wataru Endo, who spent the second half at centre-back, and Frimpong were both partly culpable when Mika Biereth levelled the scores.

open image in gallery Virgil van Dijk made his first appearance of pre-season but conceded a penalty ( PA )

Endo had come on for the great success of Liverpool’s tour of the United States. The giant Ifeanyi Ndukwe excelled again in the first half. The problem is that he is ineligible for competitive games, lacking a work permit, perhaps meaning a loan abroad beckons. In the Austrian and the Senegalese Mor Talla Ndiaye, Liverpool have two precocious 18-year-olds. Their defensive future can look secure. The concerns are about the present.

Araujo will tick some boxes; at 27, he is roughly halfway between Van Dijk and the duo of the 19-year-old Leoni and Jacquet, 21, in age and, unlike Gomez, is fit now. Liverpool need a bridge to the next generation. They hoped it would be Ibrahima Konate, but he wanted a financial package that could have felt a problem if, in a couple of years, he found himself understudying Leoni and Jacquet; or, indeed, Ndukwe.

Konate left without a proper goodbye. Harvey Elliott, who could have been gone for good, returned from his unproductive loan at Aston Villa to the loudest cheer of the afternoon. It may not herald a second coming at Anfield, however: he was the third man used at No 10, after Wirtz and then Dominik Szoboszlai, who had begun in midfield.

open image in gallery Harvey Elliott got the loudest cheer of the afternoon off the bench ( Reuters )

Even as he made 11 substitutions, there were other glimpses into Iraola’s thinking. Rio Ngumoha ended the game on the right flank. He may have to step into Salah’s shoes in more meaningful matches.

News.content:

The European Union is considering further delaying the full rollout of its entry/exit system (EES) in order to avoid added complications at its borders, according to a report.

The EU finally introduced its new border security system in stages from October last year, replacing the old process of manually stamping passports with the registration of biometric details when travellers arrive in Europe.

But the system has already faced calls to be scrapped after creating bottlenecks at airports, with a fifth of Brits now considering cancelling their European holidays this summer due to the chaos.

Industry sources told The Times that Apostolos Tzitzikostas, the commissioner responsible for negotiations over the EES with non-EU countries, has privately assured the checks will be paused.

open image in gallery Airlines warn many airports do not yet have enough biometric scanners and staff to facilitate the EES system, creating delays ( Getty/iStock )

Mr Tzitzikostas was said to be pushing to extend a derogation allowing officials to suspend the new checks past the existing deadline of 6 September for the full rollout.

And he was reported to have already made assurances to the UK that an extension is possible, having recently. met with transport secretary Heidi Alexander, according to the newspaper.

The department said last month that Ms Alexander had raised concerns about the EU’s new digital border check system with Mr Tzitzikostas during their meeting on 14 July.

Ms Alexander said in a statement at the time: “We want everyone to have the summer holidays they deserve – and yesterday’s meeting shows everyone is pulling in the same direction.

“I was reassured that the EU commissioner for transport understood the concerns of holidaymakers and recognised the need for us to work together.”

That came amid reports that passengers were missing their flights due to long queues, while Ryanair warned of “queue chaos” from the new system, which it said was not ready for full implementation.

open image in gallery Apostolos Tzitzikostas, pictured here last year, reportedly gave his representations to Heidi Alexander when they met on 14 July ( AFP/Getty )

They pointed to several popular airports including Spain’s Alicante, which they said was not ready for the checks due to “insufficient staff, kiosks and system readiness”.

Alicante-Elche Miguel Hernández airport is now preparing for a £985 million upgrade including facilities to streamline EES checks.

The EU's EES only became fully operational in April and applies to all 29 Schengen countries, most of which are EU member states, with further operations expected in the autumn.

The system requires travellers to register their biometric details, such as fingerprints and a photo, when they arrive in the EU, replacing the previous system of manually stamping passports.

EES is required for all non-EU passengers entering or exiting Schengen countries.

The British government has announced £20 million in new funding to increase the number of booths for passport checks at the country's main gateway to Europe, the Port of Dover.

The majority of the new checks will be done in EU member states, but will take place in Britain for those using the ferry through the Port of Dover or taking the train into the EU, the government said.

Tallulah Willis, the youngest daughter of Bruce Willis and Demi Moore, has married her fiancé Justin Acee in an intimate ceremony in Sun Valley, Idaho.

Tallulah wore a custom dress made by Balenciaga creative director Pierpaolo Piccioli. According to Vogue, the dress marked one of the first bridal gowns that Piccioli crafted in his role for the fashion house.

The magazine attended Tallulah’s final dress fitting the week before the wedding in a suite at the Chateau Marmont, where her mother and sisters, Rumer and Scout, were both present.

The bride told the publication that she and her husband “made a decision at the very beginning of our relationship that we were going to choose each other every day.”

She continued: “My biggest hope [for the dress] was that [it would be] something magical, but magical in a way that was unexpected, kind of like me.”

open image in gallery Tallulah Willis, the youngest daughter of Bruce Willis and Demi Moore, has married her boyfriend Justin Acee in an intimate ceremony in Sun Valley, Idaho ( Getty )

open image in gallery For her wedding day, Tallulah wore a custom dress made by Balenciaga creative director Pierpaolo Piccioli ( Getty )

The mother-of-the-bride, Ghost actor Demi Moore, told the publication that Piccioli spent four hours with them during their first meeting discussing the dress.

“The day after his first couture collection for Balenciaga, he was with us for four hours,” she said. “And I think he would have stayed there playing all day.”

The strapless column dress is crafted from silk satin and features a draped train skirt and bow at the back.

Vogue reports that the dress took 712 hours of work, including 405 hours of construction and atelier alterations. An additional nine hours were dedicated to the veil.

Tallulah, an artist and writer, announced her engagement to Acee in December, sharing an Instagram post that included a photo of the couple holding hands over a rose-petal pathway with her engagement ring visible. She captioned the post: “Everyday @justinacee.” The pair have been been dating since 2023.

Bruce and Demi are also parents to Rumer Willis, 37, and Scout Willis, 35, while the Die Hard actor shares two younger daughters with wife Emma Heming Willis: Mabel, 14, and Evelyn, 12.

Back in June 2024, Tallulah shared pictures of her and Accee spending time with her dad, who lives with frontotemporal dementia — which affects a person’s speech, personality and behavior.

Bruce receives 24-hour care and lives separately from his wife and their two young daughters.

The actor’s wife has continued to share updates about her husband’s health. In June, she said that he remembers key details about his life, including the identity of his family members around him.

“When people say, ‘Oh, you know, does he remember who you are?’ Well, he does because he doesn't have Alzheimer’s; he has FTD,” Emma said on an episode of The Bossticks podcast. “I think that's a very common misconception that, when you think of dementia, we think of memory loss.

Shaun Murphy broke Ronnie O’Sullivan’s 12-year record for the most unanswered points in a professional match as he thrashed Matthew Selt 6-0 at the China Open in Taiyuan.

Murphy, who also equalled the record of four consecutive centuries, opened the first-round tie with breaks of 18, 61, 132, 103, 139, 113 and 41 for a new record of 607 points without reply.

“It’s like a cricket score isn’t it?” Murphy told WST. “I can’t believe it, I’m over the moon.

“I knew I was close at the interval, but I didn’t want to go looking for it on any sites or anything, As a sportsperson, when you do find yourself in that bubble, in that flow, you just want to stay in it.

“Ideally I wouldn’t have had the interval, I would have just carried on. But it was a delight to play for a great crowd out there. Thrilled.

“I haven’t set many records throughout my career and I’m sure someone at some stage will come along and beat that one, but to be part of snooker history in that way is a great thrill.”

O’Sullivan set the previous record of 556 unanswered points in a 6-0 win against Ricky Walden at the 2014 Masters.

Murphy compiled successive century breaks in frames two to five and joins Mark Allen and Neil Robertson as the only players to have achieved the feat twice.

Meanwhile, O’Sullivan won six straight frames after falling 2-0 behind to beat Jackson Page 6-2, but world number one Judd Trump’s unbeaten start to the season was halted in a 6-3 defeat to Noppon Saengkham.

News.content:
For me it’s a special game, most of the players and people will be ‘it’s [just] a pre-season friendly’, but for me it’s a lot more than this. It will be the first time I have the chance to go out, to feel this stadium and I hope we can also perform well.
