World.title: Mexico’s week in review: US suspends avocado certs, fracking studies continue and Peru rift ends
World.content:
Listen to this article

President Claudia Sheinbaum’s daily press conferences set much of the week’s agenda, moving from children’s social media use to a government transparency decree, a high-profile murder, fracking policy and a diplomatic breakthrough with Peru. Economic data told a mixed story too, with a strengthening peso set against a sharp drop in Pemex profit and a battered Sinaloa economy.

Security developments also kept pace, including the arrest of a former Guerrero governor on Ayotzinapa-related charges, a jump in U.S. rewards tied to CJNG’s new leadership, and a fresh U.S. suspension of avocado certifications in Michoacán. On the public health and safety front, a UNAM cheating scandal, a UNESCO deadline to protect the vaquita and a cyclosporiasis scare linked to Riviera Maya travel all drew attention.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Economy: Peso strengthens and avocado trade swings

Mexico’s currency extended a 10-day rally to reach its strongest level since February, helped by the Bank of Mexico holding its benchmark rate at 6.5% and a weaker US dollar following a soft American jobs report. The gains came even as Pemex reported a 70% annual drop in second-quarter net profit, which the state oil company attributed to higher financial costs, tax obligations and an unfavorable exchange rate. Economic disparities varied widely by region, with Sinaloa’s economy posting the worst quarterly contraction of any Mexican state, a result economists linked to the ongoing cartel conflict in the region.

Tourism data added to the mixed picture: Tourism GDP fell 0.8% quarter-over-quarter in the first three months of the year, according to INEGI, driven by a 5.9% quarterly drop in spending by foreign visitors, even as domestic tourism consumption rose 0.5%.

Mexico’s avocado trade also had a volatile week. New data showed exports to the U.S. jumped 35% in the first quarter compared to the previous year, according to Sader. Days later, however, the United States suspended avocado export certifications in Michoacán, citing an unspecified “threat against U.S. interests” — the third such suspension in just over four years. Michoacán’s governor deployed additional state security operatives and the Defense Ministry sent more than 1,500 soldiers to the region in response.

Energy: Government edges toward fracking while banning it in Mexico’s top basin

A government expert committee tasked with assessing “sustainable fracking” recommended prohibiting hydraulic fracturing in the Tampico-Misantla basin, Mexico’s largest-potential shale region, citing environmental, social and biodiversity concerns. Sheinbaum said her government would respect that recommendation, which she reaffirmed at Friday’s mañanera.

However, the committee recommended continued evaluation of two other northern basins. Reuters reported that pilot projects in Coahuila and Tamaulipas could begin as soon as next month if approved, as Mexico looks to reduce its reliance on natural gas imports from the United States.

Security: Pressure builds on cartels and past officials

U.S. authorities raised the reward for CJNG’s new leader, Juan Carlos Valencia González, to $25 million following the February death of cartel founder “El Mencho,” as part of more than $100 million in reward offers and new visa restrictions. Domestically, federal agents dismantled four illicit fuel processing centers in San Luis Potosí, Hidalgo and Morelos, seizing roughly 1 million liters of fuel. In Sinaloa, Sheinbaum acknowledged the murder of content creator César Gastélum, the ninth social media personality killed in the state since 2024. And in a case tied to one of Mexico’s most notorious unsolved crimes, federal authorities arrested former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre on charges of concealing video evidence related to the 2014 disappearance of 43 Ayotzinapa students; Sheinbaum said the arrest was not politically motivated.

Public health, environment and education

Sheinbaum laid the cornerstone for a new IMSS hospital in Oaxaca, part of a three-facility “Health City” complex the government frames as a step toward its planned Universal Health Service. And after the U.K. reported dozens of cyclosporiasis cases among travelers, Mexico stepped up health inspections at Riviera Maya hotels, while officials said the country has not been identified as the outbreak’s source.

Officials at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) confirmed that nearly 60,000 applicants must retake its entrance exam after widespread cheating undermined its first-ever online exam.

Separately, UNESCO gave Mexico until February to show concrete action to protect the critically endangered vaquita porpoise, of which only seven to 10 are believed to remain.

Diplomacy and governance

Sheinbaum signed a decree aimed at strengthening federal government transparency, which officials said would compel departments to disclose more information following the 2024 elimination of the INAI watchdog agency.

On the diplomatic front, Sheinbaum announced that Mexico and Peru would restore relations severed since November, after former Peruvian Prime Minister Bettsy Chávez was granted safe passage from asylum in Mexico’s Lima embassy.

Looking ahead

The coming weeks will test several threads left open this week: whether Mexican and U.S. officials can resolve the security concerns behind the avocado certification suspension, whether President Sheinbaum’s panel of experts finds acceptable conditions in northern Mexico to move fracking pilot projects forward, and how UNAM’s rescheduled in-person exams — set for mid-to-late August — play out after the cheating controversy. Mexico also faces UNESCO’s February deadline on vaquita protections and continued scrutiny of Sinaloa’s cartel-driven economic slowdown.

World.title: A celebration of Mexican artist Arturo García Bustos, 100 years after his birth
World.content:
On Aug. 8, 1926, a child was born in the heart of Mexico City. Although he grew up to explore many places, his heart remained where his passion for art was first sparked, and he passed away in his house in Coyoacán on April 7, 2017.

Arturo García Bustos is recognized for his role in Mexican art history, notably as a student of Frida Kahlo and a dedicated artist whose legacy continues to inspire.

“The love that Frida instilled in us towards Mexican culture, towards our roots and popular customs, is still alive and present in my work,” the artist stated in a 1977 interview with El Día, underscoring his lifelong dedication to Mexican identity.

A childhood in the city

One cannot grow up in Mexico City without it leaving a mark. García Bustos was well aware of this, recalling fondly that as a primary school student, he would watch Diego Rivera working on his murals at the Secretaría de Educación Pública (Ministry of Public Education).

Little did he know that he would eventually marry one of Rivera’s close collaborators, Rina Lazo, and become closer to the master muralist than he could have ever imagined.

Living downtown put him at the center of a growing metropolis, where he attended public concerts, frequented local libraries and developed a keen eye for observing urban life.

A rebellious spirit

Ever the rebel, García Bustos broke away from the strict, rigid norms of the Academia de San Carlos, Mexico’s most prestigious art academy at the time. He transferred to La Esmeralda — a decision that altered his life forever. There, he not only found his true mentors, but also met Guatemalan-Mexican artist Rina Lazo, the woman he would marry and spend his life alongside.

In contrast with the San Carlos Academy, Frida Kahlo didn’t teach through theory. She avoided a clinical approach to creation, favoring a sensitive, vibrant perspective on the artistic process instead.

She challenged her students to observe the world deeply, asking them to count the subtle colors hidden in everyday objects. When her failing health made her commute to La Esmeralda impossible, she transformed her beloved Casa Azul in Coyoacán into a creative sanctuary. It was here that Arturo García Bustos became one of the four devoted pupils known as “Los Fridos.”

Kahlo’s mentorship catalyzed a breakthrough that launched García Bustos into the Mexican art scene. Kahlo actively championed her students’ careers, securing them local mural projects — like painting the walls of a nearby pulquería — and introducing their work to leading Mexican intellectuals.

García Bustos, the militant

La Esmeralda also connected Arturo to artist collectives that defined the trajectory of his work: the Taller de Gráfica Popular (TGP) and Artistas Jóvenes Revolucionarios. These groups were not merely social clubs; they were part of a broader movement given voice by printmakers and painters who proudly viewed themselves as visual working-class laborers.

Bustos quickly adopted graphic art as one of his primary media. At just 18 years old, he joined the Taller de Gráfica Popular — founded by Leopoldo Méndez, Luis Arenal and Pablo O’Higgins — to design flyers, posters and newspapers that documented global struggles and amplified labor union demands.

Through the TGP, García Bustos deepened his understanding of both printmaking and sociopolitical activism. Members divided their time equally between pulling prints and attending political assemblies or protests, bridging the gap between art and labor.

Simultaneously, young creators were forging their own spaces. The Artistas Jóvenes Revolucionarios collective brought together students seeking to display politically engaged artwork. Bypassing traditional galleries and museums, they exhibited in public parks and markets to invite direct dialogue with everyday citizens.

Inevitably, a teacher

Following in Kahlo’s footsteps, Arturo dedicated years of his life to education. Two institutions stand out in his teaching journey: the Escuela Nacional de Artes Plásticas in Guatemala and the Escuela de Bellas Artes de Oaxaca.

He was invited to Guatemala by writer and diplomat Luis Cardoza y Aragón — a move warmly supported by his wife, Rina Lazo. During his residency, he established a printmaking workshop that produced socially critical work, though political upheaval soon forced him to return to Mexico.

García Bustos shaped generations of talent, including renowned artist Francisco Toledo, through his dedicated work at the Escuela de Bellas Artes in Oaxaca, inspiring respect for his mentorship.

Artwork

There are two remarkable paths that García Bustos followed — or rather cultivated — throughout his career: muralism and printmaking. Perhaps at first sight they may seem far from one another, but they shared a common interest in getting art to the people. While the former is usually displayed publicly, the latter is, by nature, easy to reproduce repeatedly.

Regarding the first discipline, more than 10 murals can be attributed — individually or collectively — to García Bustos. His motifs always revolve around Mexican history, Indigenous traditions and social justice. Although all his work has been equally relevant, certain pieces have sparked debate and become landmarks where they were created.

In Oaxaca

One of his most significant murals, “Las Siete Regiones de Oaxaca,” created for the National Museum of Anthropology, exemplifies his dedication to Mexican history and cultural identity.

When Arturo created the murals for the Palacio de Gobierno de Oaxaca in 1980, there was much discussion about whether a non-Oaxacan artist should paint them; one of the main opponents was Oaxacan artist Rufino Tamayo. The protests eventually ceased once supporters argued that García Bustos had already given a great deal to the state through his teaching at the Escuela de Bellas Artes in Oaxaca.

In Mexico City

Additionally, he painted a stunning mural that thousands of people see every day at the Metro station Universidad in Mexico City, located at the heart of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México: “The University on the Threshold of the 21st Century.” In this piece, Arturo journeys through the different means of knowledge and education in Mexico. He also portrays key historical figures such as Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, his mentor Frida Kahlo and his lifelong partner, Rina Lazo.

Finally, one of his last murals adorns the walls of the Casa de Cultura de Azcapotzalco in Mexico City. Here, García Bustos not only showcases his technical expertise but also enriches a community cultural space with iconic moments from Mexican history.

On the 100th anniversary of his birth, Arturo García Bustos has become an undeniably influential figure in modern Mexican art, far beyond his status as one of Los Fridos. Ultimately, his legacy enriches Mexico’s public spaces and the generations of artists he inspired alongside Rina Lazo.

Lydia Leija is a linguist, journalist and visual storyteller. She has directed three feature films, and her audiovisual work has been featured in national and international media. She’s been part of National Geographic, Muy Interesante and Cosmopolitan.

World.title: Beyond the lechero: Veracruz’s new wave of coffee culture
World.content:
When I first decided to leave the San Francisco Bay Area in California to live in Xalapa, Veracruz — the city where both of my parents once immigrated from decades ago, and where my mom eventually moved back to live — I never anticipated how much I would fall in love with one of Mexico’s best-kept secrets: Jarocho coffee.

The state’s adoration for, and history of, producing some of Mexico’s best coffee dates back centuries. This is, after all, where coffee cultivation began with the arrival of Europeans in the 1700s. While living here, I’ve been able to travel along the oldest coffee-producing trails on the continent, sipping my way through it all, and visiting coffee plantations to learn more about the process and conditions for cultivating coffee and its environmental impacts in modern times (spoiler: it’s harder than ever for producers to keep up with the global demand and maintain their practices from the past).

The rich coffee culture of Veracruz

In Mexico’s entirety, no state boasts the same pedigree of rich coffee lineage and ongoing traditions as deeply, and perhaps as invisibly, as Veracruz. Nowhere is that notion more evident than in the state’s largest city: the actual port itself.

Of course, Jarocho coffee is by no means completely unheard of or brand new, by any stretch of the imagination, particularly for those in the know. The sight of a “lechero” pouring frothy milk into a cup of espresso at El Gran Café de la Parroquia is a classic image of the Veracruz experience going back to 1808, when the cafe first opened as a tiny operation in front of the Parroquia de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción.

Now, it represents one of Mexico’s most iconic coffee rituals. Here’s how it works: patrons tap their glass with a spoon; a formally dressed lechero comes bustling over with a steaming pot of milk; the lechero evinces showmanship by pouring the milk from a spout at an impressive height, never spilling a drop. It may seem gimmicky for some, but throughout my life, it has always represented the Jarocho way of drinking coffee.

Café traditionalism

In addition to El Gran Café de la Parroquia (which eventually split into two separate factions due to ownership disputes in the 1990s), Gran Café del Portal in Veracruz’s historic center is also worth visiting for its colonial-era charm and sense of coffee traditionalism. Indeed, the port of Veracruz’s reputational coffee heritage has carried over into other parts of Mexico over the years, too; the most popular café in Coyoacán is named El Jarocho, which opened in 1953, and ships its coffee beans by the truckloads directly from Huatusco, Veracruz.

And yet, while becoming an intrinsic part of a classic tourist experience in Veracruz, the city has not always found a way to merge its glorious coffee past with its ongoing present and future. Until now.

A new generation of cafés

Currently, the specialty coffee scene in the port of Veracruz is booming in unseen ways, as a new wave of coffeemakers and baristas has entered the mix with a more contemporary approach, offering a cool range of Veracruz’s flavorful past in an aesthetic, renovated context. In just the past year and a half that I’ve lived in the state of Veracruz, I’ve noticed an uptick of youthful cafés in the puerto; it seems that every time I go for a weekend outing with my family, another one springs up.

So here are just a few of those cafes that should be added to your list. The next time you decide to visit Mexico’s oldest and most historically important port city — where imbibing a cup of coffee in the midday swelter is a way of life — you can experience its coffee renaissance for yourself.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Singular Coffee Roasters (@singular.coffee.roasters)

Located directly across the street from Playa de Oro, right on the border of Boca del Rio — a ritzier suburb a few miles away from the industrial center of Veracruz — Singular Coffee Roasters in many ways embodies the next generation of coffeemakers in the city. In addition to having a pristine view of the beach, where the nearby ocean scenically blows palm trees along the main avenue, the vibe is funky and hip, and the menu is top-notch.

Enjoy a tampiqueña de res (a thin cut of beef served with salsa, salad greens and beans) alongside an orange cold brew, a maracuyita (cold brew mixed with mashed passion fruit) or a matcha frappe. Or, keep it simple, and order a locally sourced cup of filtered coffee — with the option of adding coconut milk for an extra 20 pesos. Either way, it’ll be a refreshing way to start off your day before hitting the nearby Gulf’s waters to cool off from the oppressive weight of the year-round heat.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by IMPETUS – Casa Tostadora de Café (@impetus.mx)

With three locations sprinkled throughout the city, Impetus has become the “it” café in town. Recently named as one of seven finalists in Mexico’s nationwide Expo Café, the brand is certainly of the highest caliber, and the interior decor and design of each café matches the high-grade taste in each cup. Though their original location has been around for 10 years now, they’ve still retained the title as Veracruz’s leading specialty coffee purveyors with a seasonally changing menu. Available in multiple price tiers ascending from lowest to highest (coffee of the day, excellent or extraordinary), they’re known for their fine-tuned brewing methods. In true Veracruz fashion, you can cool off with a granizado de olla (shaved ice poured over with café de olla) or a chilled bottle of housemade cascarita (a fruity, tea-like beverage made by steeping the dried husks of a coffee cherry in water).

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ETHOS Casa de Café (@ethos_casadecafe)

Small but mighty, this bite-sized café (it’s a small room that comfortably seats around 10 people, not counting the limited sidewalk seating available outside) was named as one of the Top 100 Coffee Shops in North America, Central America and the Caribbean islands. Aside from their regular pours — which are exceptional — they offer cold brews infused with in-house ginger ale, coffee liqueur frappes and dulce de leche espressos, among other inventive options like the Blue Velvet (a concoction of blue butterfly pea flower extract, lavender, organic vanilla and milk).

View this post on Instagram A post shared by VOLADOR – Café de Altura (@volador.mx)

Recognized as a two-time Expo Café winner for producing the best coffee in Mexico, this outpost can be found on a vibrant strip in Colonia Reforma (which, for my money, is the coolest and most diverse neighborhood in the state of Veracruz, replete with stylish bars, cafés, taquerias, Korean ramen, smash burgers, Middle Eastern dining, pizzerias and more, all connected by a tree-lined walking path that leads straight to the beach). Volador is the unequivocal king of coffee in this area, with a spacious environment and outdoor patio seating to accompany its vegan food options, salads and — for the over-18 crowd — carajillos (espresso and coffee liqueur) in mazapan or horchata varietals.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Avi Café (@avicafe_)

Specializing in brunch and sweet treats — in addition to their selection of coffee and teas — this dog-friendly café is charming and sprightly. Another of Colonia Reforma’s highlights, it opened at the end of 2024 and has added to Veracruz’s rising cafe presence. A pistachio tarta vasca (a dense Basque-style cheesecake) is ideally partnered with a tri-colored strawberry matcha, an iced taro or a classic espresso cortado.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by @habibicafeteria

The latest newcomer to Veracruz’s growing and diversifying coffee scene, Habibi opened its doors earlier this summer and added something completely fresh and rare to the port city’s culinary sphere: a Turkish-inspired café. Found in the ever-trendy Reforma neighborhood, the decor here is a bit over the top and kitschy, but the spirit of the coffee and food is unique and notable. Order a Turkish coffee (which is brewed in hot sand) and, if you’re hungering or have a sweet tooth, add a side of gold-dusted dessert — or grab a loaded shawarma de pollo — and stay for the fun of it all. Pro tip: don’t forget the plátano macho-stuffed kibbeh.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Aquí si volvemos (@aquisivolvemos)

The tropical abundance of Veracruz’s ingredients reigns supreme at DeLirio. Take your pick of orange espressos, pineapple cold brews, maracuya cheesecakes, watermelon agua frescas, chilled cucumbers and lime frappes, and so much more. Despite its colorful vibrancy on the menu, it retains an understated interior style: An elegant, minimalist architecture highlighted by its mid-century-inspired curved walls and wicker chairs — all working in harmony to accentuate this chic café in (you guessed it) Colonia Reforma.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020) and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: MND launches new series on personal finance
World.content:
The team at Mexico News Daily is always trying to think of new content ideas to help better educate and inform our readers about Mexico. A few recent examples include our Expat Safety Perceptions Index, the MND Mexico Healthcare Survey, and the Sheinbaum, Mexico Economy, and Peso Indexes.

As we have been working on these content ideas over the past few months, we have received feedback from readers on other ideas, and we have identified some additional gaps as well. One of them is to create an index that focuses more on Mexico’s social progress (or lack of) versus more economically focused indicators. We are actively working on that one — stay tuned!

Another big gap we identified was regarding the whole issue of money and personal finance in Mexico. It occurred to us that there is often a real gap in knowledge when it comes to money in Mexico. Many people who are extremely sophisticated financially in their home country oftentimes don’t even have a bank account in Mexico. Others that I have met have little more than a local basic checking account with a debit card. Still others lose significant amounts of money on currency conversion.

The light bulb really went off when we were reviewing the results of the Expat Safety Perceptions Index. The data of our survey showed us that most expats/foreigners have not had personal safety issues and in fact, for the most part, feel very safe in Mexico. From a personal safety perspective, most feel pretty good. But that got us thinking and asking questions like:

1. What financial issues have you had in Mexico?

2. What are the financial risks the immigrants face here?

3. What are common mistakes that immigrants make with money here?

4. How many MND readers have been victims of a financial crime in Mexico?

5. What can you do to protect your finances in Mexico?

We believe that this is an extremely important topic and there is much to be learned and applied. As a result, Mexico News Daily will be going “all in” on this topic. We will start with a survey that we will be asking thousands of expats in Mexico to take. The results of this survey will be shared with our readers and will also help guide and define the topics of a new weekly series of “Mexico and My Money,” beginning next week. In this series, we will be covering everything from common mistakes made to best practices for protecting and growing your money in Mexico. We will cover topics like banking, exchanging money, rental income, investing, and dealing with contractors and local service providers.

Our goal is neither to scare you nor lead you to a false sense of security, but rather to provide you with the information, best practices and lessons learned of others to help you best manage your money in Mexico. Stay tuned, I am certain that we are all going to learn a lot from this survey and series.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Costa Rica Studies Monorail or Tram for Main Airport
World.content:
Costa Rican transportation officials are looking for European funding to study a public transit connection between Juan Santamaría International Airport and the planned electric train network. The proposal would connect the airport terminal with the railway line near Río Segundo, removing one of the main barriers facing travelers who want to use public transportation between the San Jose airport and the Greater Metropolitan Area.

Officials are considering several possible systems, including a monorail or light rail service. The technical studies would determine which option is best suited to the short connection, as well as its cost, design and possible construction timeline. The Costa Rican Railway Institute (Incofer), is developing the plan with the Ministry of Public Works and Transportation and Aeris, the company that manages Juan Santamaría International Airport.

The agencies hope to finance the studies through non-repayable cooperation funds from the European Union. However, the funding has not yet been confirmed, and authorities have not established how much the studies or eventual construction would cost. Transportation officials expect to get approval to begin the studies in December 2026.

The airport connection would link to the planned TIBI electric train project. From Río Segundo, passengers could continue by rail toward Alajuela, Heredia, San José and Cartago. Officials also want the transit system coordinated with the planned expansion of the highway between San José and San Ramón. That road project includes a new interchange in front of the airport designed to bring together cars, buses, trains and other forms of transportation.

A survey conducted among Costa Rican and international travelers found that 82 percent of respondents would be willing to use a public transportation connection at the airport if one were available. Juan Santamaría currently has public buses serving San José, Alajuela and other destinations, but the terminal does not have a direct rail connection. Many arriving passengers instead depend on taxis, ride-hailing services, rental cars or private hotel transfers.

The gap is particularly noticeable for visitors traveling into San José, where congestion along the General Cañas Highway can make travel times unpredictable. A rail connection has been discussed previously, but the latest proposal remains at an early stage. No technology has been selected, no construction funding has been approved and no opening date has been announced.

The studies will determine whether the project is technically and financially practical before the government decides whether to move ahead.

World.title: FIFA Defends Gianni Infantino Amid Leadership Crisis
World.content:
FIFA has accused critics of waging a “concerted and ongoing effort” to undermine the organization and its president, Gianni Infantino, as the crisis surrounding his leadership continues to deepen. The governing body issued a strongly worded statement Saturday defending Infantino following the collapse of a controversial proposal to bring private investors into FIFA’s World Cup commercial business.

The plan triggered fierce opposition from several major football organizations and has left Infantino facing boycott threats, calls for his resignation and growing questions about his bid for another term as FIFA president. Infantino, who has led FIFA since 2016, is seeking reelection at the organization’s congress in March 2027. FIFA’s 211 member associations will ultimately decide whether he remains in office.

European football’s governing body UEFA has emerged as one of his strongest critics. Despite FIFA abandoning the private investment proposal, UEFA has said the decision alone is not enough to restore confidence in Infantino’s leadership. The dispute has escalated to the point that European football officials have threatened to boycott FIFA competitions, including World Cups.

New Allegations Add to Pressure

Infantino faced another controversy Friday after The Telegraph reported allegations involving his time as UEFA general secretary between 2009 and 2016. The British newspaper alleged that Infantino used his influence to help secure the promotion of a female UEFA employee with whom he was reportedly involved in a personal relationship.

Infantino has categorically denied the allegations. The Telegraph also reported that the employee later received a six-figure payment when she left UEFA, along with approximately €50,000 ($57,800) toward an MBA program. UEFA has acknowledged that a payment was made to the former employee and that expenses connected with an MBA program were also covered.

FIFA did not specifically identify the Telegraph report in its Saturday statement but pushed back strongly against recent coverage surrounding its president. “Recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning FIFA and its president,” the organization said. FIFA added that speculation and insinuation should not be treated as fact and said it would challenge inaccurate or misleading reporting.

FIFA Warns Against Attempts to Remove Infantino

FIFA also emphasized that any effort to replace Infantino must follow the organization’s statutes and established election procedures. “Those who do not have the support of FIFA’s Member Associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through FIFA’s established democratic processes,” the organization said.

FIFA’s leadership reaffirmed its support for Infantino during a crisis meeting in Morocco earlier this week. The organization also apologized to its 211 member associations for mistakes in the way the private investment proposal was handled, acknowledging that members should have been more involved in the process.

That apology has done little to settle the dispute. UEFA has said it has lost confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation president Lise Klaveness went further Friday and publicly called for him to resign. Klaveness, one of Infantino’s most outspoken critics in international football, said he no longer has the institutional trust necessary to lead FIFA.

Her name has also been mentioned as a possible future candidate for the FIFA presidency, although she has played down speculation about running.

Infantino Retains Support Outside Europe

Despite the growing pressure in Europe, Infantino continues to receive significant backing elsewhere. The Confederation of African Football has publicly supported his leadership, while South American governing body Conmebol has rejected attempts to remove him outside FIFA’s established electoral process.

Infantino traveled to Cali, Colombia, on Friday for the inauguration of newly elected right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella, where Conmebol president Alejandro Domínguez reiterated his support. Domínguez said Infantino’s work at FIFA should not be ignored and called for disagreements within world football to be resolved through dialogue.

The competing statements highlight a widening divide within international football ahead of the 2027 FIFA presidential election. For years, Infantino appeared to be heading toward another term with relatively little resistance. The collapse of the private investment plan and the increasingly public confrontation between FIFA and UEFA have now turned what once looked like a straightforward reelection campaign into one of the most serious leadership crises of his decade in charge.

World.title: Costa Rica Reports Renewed Increase in COVID-19 Cases
World.content:
COVID-19 has once again become the most widely circulating respiratory virus detected in Costa Rica, as health officials urge residents to take basic precautions amid an increase in cases and hospitalizations. The latest epidemiological surveillance places COVID-19 ahead of rhinovirus and parainfluenza among respiratory viruses currently circulating here.

During epidemiological week 29, covering July 13 through July 19, Costa Rica recorded 126 confirmed COVID-19 cases, up from 94 the previous week. That represents an increase of about 34%. Hospitalizations also climbed, with 29 COVID-19 patients receiving hospital care compared with 18 the previous week, an increase of roughly 56%. Five deaths associated with COVID-19 were reported during the same epidemiological week.

The figures remain far below the levels Costa Rica experienced during the height of the pandemic, and there is currently no national health alert for respiratory illnesses. However, the change in circulation has prompted renewed attention as several respiratory viruses spread simultaneously.

Costa Rica has recorded more than 771,000 cases of respiratory illness so far this year, a broader figure that includes illnesses caused by multiple viruses rather than COVID-19 alone. Children, older adults and people with chronic health conditions remain among those considered most vulnerable to complications from respiratory infections.

Health authorities are recommending many of the familiar measures used to reduce respiratory infections: keeping vaccinations current, washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes and choosing well-ventilated spaces when possible. People experiencing respiratory symptoms are also being encouraged to avoid crowded activities and limit close contact with vulnerable relatives or friends until they recover.

The renewed circulation of COVID-19 comes during Costa Rica’s rainy season, when respiratory illnesses can become more noticeable as people spend more time indoors and several viruses circulate at the same time. For residents and travelers, the latest numbers do not signal a return to pandemic-era restrictions. There have been no announcements of renewed mask mandates, travel requirements or widespread restrictions connected to the current increase.

Instead, the emphasis remains on individual precautions, particularly for people at greater risk of serious illness. Health officials continue to monitor COVID-19 alongside influenza, rhinovirus, parainfluenza and other respiratory illnesses to identify changes in circulation and hospital demand.

World.title: Where You Can Fly Nonstop to Costa Rica This High Season
World.content:
Getting to Costa Rica is about to get easier from a lot more places. Fourteen new or expanded nonstop flights start between October and March, and several of them connect cities that have never had a direct flight here. One heavily promoted route has already been cancelled, and it is worth knowing which. If you are planning a trip for the high season, or you have family flying down to visit, this is the list you need.

Every route below is confirmed by the airline, with start dates, days of the week and aircraft where those have been published. The expansion follows a strong year for arrivals. Between January and June, 1,605,360 travelers landed in Costa Rica by air, up 7.8% over the same six months of 2025 and the best first half on record.

New flights to San Jose

Las Vegas is off the table. Southwest announced a daily overnight Las Vegas to San Jose route in February, pushed the launch from October to November, then cancelled it in July before a single flight operated. The airline cited fuel costs and a decision to use its aircraft more efficiently, since an overnight leaves a plane parked in Costa Rica for hours. If you were waiting on that one, stop waiting.

That leaves the western United States where it was. From Nevada, Arizona and most of California you are still connecting through Houston, Miami or another gateway to reach Costa Rica.

Breeze Airways arrives from Tampa on October 3. This is the airline’s first-ever service to Costa Rica and makes the country its fifth international destination. Flights run Wednesdays and Saturdays on an Airbus A220 seating 137. Tampa has not had a direct link to San Jose in more than 25 years.

Air Transat starts Quebec City on December 15, once a week. Unlike most of the winter additions, this one is permanent rather than seasonal, and it brings the number of Canadian cities with direct flights to Costa Rica to seven.

Porter connects Toronto Pearson from December 2 through April 30, four flights a week on an Embraer E195-E2 seating 132. The aircraft has no middle seats.

Southwest adds Austin on March 13, 2027, Saturdays only. It is the only nonstop between Central Texas and San Jose. The outbound leaves Austin at 10:25 a.m. and lands at 2:05 p.m., with the return departing at 3:05 p.m. Tickets are already on sale.

New flights to Guanacaste

Liberia keeps pulling ahead. Daniel Oduber Quiros handled its busiest quarter ever in early 2026, and airlines have noticed. Air Canada flies Vancouver from December 13 through April 12, Mondays and Thursdays on a Boeing 737 MAX 8 seating 177. Canadian traffic through Liberia grew 28% in the first half of this year, which is the main reason so many of these routes point north.

WestJet adds Ottawa from December 20 through April 4, Sundays, on a 737 MAX 8 seating 174. Worth knowing before you shop: Porter already flies Ottawa to Liberia weekly through the winter, so from December you have two nonstop options on that route rather than one.

United flies Washington-Dulles daily from December 17 through January 4. Note how short that window is. It is a holiday-season route, not a winter-long one, and if you want it you should book early. The aircraft is a Boeing 737 MAX 9 with 179 seats including 20 in business.

That route also completes something unusual. United will now serve Liberia from all seven of its US hubs, alongside Newark, Denver, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Houston and Chicago. Delta returns to New York JFK from December 19 through April 10, Saturdays only, on an Airbus A321neo seating 194. Delta last flew this route in 2016, and it currently offers no service at all between New York City and Costa Rica.

Southwest adds Nashville from February 13 to March 6, 2027, Saturdays, on a 737 MAX 8. That is a four-week window, the shortest on this list.

Costa Rica gets its first flights from Poland

The most unexpected addition is a charter series. Rainbow Tours and LOT Polish Airlines will run eleven flights into Liberia on a Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner seating 251, the first direct air link between Poland and Costa Rica. Warsaw Chopin operates weekly from October 8 to 29. Katowice takes over weekly from November 5 to December 17.

These are charter operations sold through a tour operator, so you will not find them on a standard flight search. If you have family in Poland planning a visit, that is the booking route.

More Seats from Europe

Three European carriers are adding frequencies rather than new destinations, which matters if you have struggled to find a seat on a specific day.

British Airways moves to Heathrow on October 25 and goes from three to five weekly flights through March, operating Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays on a Boeing 787-8. If you connect onward in Europe, this is the change that matters most. Heathrow is the airline’s main hub, and it has never had scheduled service to Costa Rica or anywhere in Central America until now.

Lufthansa moves from three to five weekly Frankfurt flights from October 25 to March 27, operating Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. The days change as well as the count, so check yours. The route currently runs Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays. Lufthansa is also switching to a Boeing 787-9 with its newer Allegris cabin.

Iberojet adds a third weekly Madrid flight on Thursdays from late November. The airline expects to make it permanent across 2027 and 2028.

The full list

Airline Route Starts Days Southwest Las Vegas to San Jose Cancelled Dropped before launch Breeze Tampa to San Jose Oct 3 Wed, Sat LOT (charter) Warsaw to Liberia Oct 8 to 29 Weekly British Airways London Heathrow to San Jose Oct 25 (3 to 5 weekly) Tue, Wed, Fri, Sat, Sun Lufthansa Frankfurt to San Jose Oct 25 (3 to 5 weekly) Mon, Wed, Fri, Sat, Sun LOT (charter) Katowice to Liberia Nov 5 to Dec 17 Weekly Iberojet Madrid to San Jose Late Nov (2 to 3 weekly) Adds Thu Porter Toronto to San Jose Dec 2 to Apr 30 4 weekly Air Canada Vancouver to Liberia Dec 13 to Apr 12 Mon, Thu Air Transat Quebec City to San Jose Dec 15 Weekly United Washington-Dulles to Liberia Dec 17 to Jan 4 Daily Delta New York JFK to Liberia Dec 19 to Apr 10 Sat WestJet Ottawa to Liberia Dec 20 to Apr 4 Sun Southwest Nashville to Liberia Feb 13 to Mar 6 Sat Southwest Austin to San Jose Mar 13, 2027 Sat

Before you book

Pick your airport before you pick your flight. Liberia puts you within a short drive of Tamarindo, Nosara, Playas del Coco, Papagayo, Flamingo and Santa Teresa. San Jose is better for the Caribbean side, the Central Valley, the southern Pacific and anywhere you need a domestic connection. Landing at the wrong one can add four or five hours of driving to your first day.

Watch the end dates as closely as the start dates. Several of these routes run for weeks rather than months, and a return flight that does not exist yet is a common way to get stuck paying for a connection you did not plan. Liberia also operates only between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m., so late arrivals are not an option there regardless of what a search engine shows you.

Seasonal routes get pulled when they do not sell. If a specific one matters to your plans, booking it early does more than save money, it helps keep the route on the schedule. That is also the argument for travel insurance on a seasonal route. If an airline drops the flight or shifts the schedule after you have booked hotels and tours around it, a policy that covers trip interruption is what stands between you and paying twice.

World.title: BTL – From Beginning to End: Ashcroft Gets The Last Laugh?
World.content:
BTL – From Beginning to End: Ashcroft Gets The Last Laugh?

The views expressed in this article are those of the author and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Adam Flowers: From the very beginning in 1988, when the Esquivel-UDP first opened BTL to public shareholding, perennial Belizean boogeyman Lord Michael Ashcroft slowly sank his fangs into the company; and now nearly 40 years, several administrations, half a billion dollars and countless controversies later including this latest; he is taking one last bite of the BTL pie and having the last laugh.

After tooth and nail, BTL was finally nationalized in 2009; at an enormous gross nationalization-related outlay to Belize of roughly $564 Million. And even that figure does not necessarily represent the complete bill. Once years of accumulated interest, legal and arbitration expenses, tax concessions and other costs arising from the wider BTL saga are considered, contemporary estimates placed the overall cost closer to $700 Million. Opposition parliamentarians were already warning by 2017 that the final figure could approach $700 Million, though no single audited Government accounting has established $700 Million as an exact final nationalization cost. More than half the big B. The cost associated with liberation from Ashcroft’s near-total control of Belize’s telecommunications sector; only now to once again intertwine itself with Ashcroft-linked interests through the Speednet acquisition through 2030 for almost another $100 Million.

And are we surprised that the maturity of the amortization schedule coincides with the year in which the next general election cycle would culminate in 2030, if the current term runs its full course? It is an $80 Million acquisition with total scheduled payments of $91.46 Million, and for the Briceño shareholders, this represents an estimated total $20.59 Million based on amortization and interest terms for their 22.51% stake in Speednet, if the seller notes and interest are allocated proportionately to their shareholding.

Essentially, once principal amortization begins; BTL will need to pay Speednet shareholders about $5.5 Million every 3 months or almost $22 Million a year with a total interest of $11.46 Million. And the success of the deal hinges on many IFs: Like IF Smart is even worth $80 Million; IF Speednet’s annual free cash flow will meet the $22 million amortization requirement; or IF BTL will need to cover any shortfall; and IF BTL’s projections of cost savings and “synergies” will materialize.

Usually, if a deal seems too good to be true, it normally is. Speednet shareholders assert the company is viable for the foreseeable future but have agreed to unexpectedly favorable terms to BTL; to finance the $80 Million at 4.5% interest with the first year as interest only followed by 16 quarterly principal-and-interest amortization payments.

And as BTL completes the merger; certain jobs could become redundant, integration costs will increase; and in a one-company national mobile market regulated by a Public Utilities Commission (PUC) of Government appointees, who can guarantee that consumers will not eventually face higher service costs to meet payment demands?

It could be Lord Ashcroft’s parting gift to BTL for all the memories. BTL was incorporated in 1987 and by 1988, Ashcroft-alliance company Carlisle Holdings had already bought around 9% of shares. By 1992, Carlisle bought another 15% giving a 24% stake and in 1993, the outgoing George Price Administration gave Ashcroft/Carlisle “permitted person” status, effectively allowing Ashcroft to hold more than 25% of the company, despite the 25% cap that otherwise applied to ordinary private shareholders under the company’s original Articles of Association.

When the Manuel Esquivel UDP came to office later in 1993, it refused to honor the exemption and up to 1998, Ashcroft was blocked from exercising his permitted person status even though he continued buying shares, though they could not be registered against the 25% ownership cap. By the time the PUP under Said Musa came back to power, the stage was set. In 2001, Carlisle Holdings bought MCI’s roughly 25% block, bringing its total shareholding to 48.4%. Carlisle then bought about another 3% from other BTL shareholders, bringing its total to roughly 52%. The Musa administration allowed Carlisle to register all its shareholdings giving it majority control of BTL. Government even appointed Ashcroft Chairman of the Board.

The Telecommunications Act of 2002 provided for competition and new licenses and in 2002 Speednet is incorporated. By late 2003, Ashcroft agrees to sell his majority stake in BTL. Enter Jefferey Prosser. In 2004, Government buys Carlisle’s shares for US$57 Million, combines them with other shares and sells roughly 84% of BTL in a transaction worth approximately US$89.7 Million. However, by 2005, Prosser defaults on a US$57 Million payment and GOB takes back control of majority shares.

By the time Government finished disposing those shares, Ashcroft’s companies once again re-emerged as the controlling interest of BTL. By March 2005, SMART goes live. And as history records, in September 2005, Prime Minister Said Musa signs the infamous, secret Accommodation Agreement; guaranteeing BTL a minimum 15% annual rate of return, favorable tax treatment and import-duty concessions, restricted the granting of telecommunications licenses to any new competitors other than SMART and limited government interference. The Agreement did not merely give BTL favorable tax treatment. It also created a mechanism through which shortfalls under the guaranteed 15% rate of return could ultimately be set off against taxes otherwise payable to Government, including business tax, while also providing specific tax exemptions. By 2008, millions of dollars in taxes had already been offset under the arrangements. Years later, Barrow’s own Government placed an extraordinary value on getting rid of the Agreement: in 2016 Barrow put the savings attributable to its elimination at around $202 Million, and later described almost a quarter-billion dollars of the BTL award as being attributable to the Accommodation Agreement itself. Of incredible note, during this period of time, the Leader of the Opposition also acted as attorney for Ashcroft’s ECom in BTL litigation during the months leading to the signing of the Accommodation Agreement.

Between 2006-2007, the assets, rights, obligations and liabilities of Belize Telecommunications Limited were transferred to its successor, Belize Telemedia Limited and then the Dean Barrow administration comes to power in a red wave, owed significantly to public fallout over some of the very BTL deals made by the former PUP administrations. Barrow rejects the Accommodation Agreement and in August 2009 moves to nationalize BTL. But there is an extraordinary footnote to that morning. On August 24, 2009, the very day Barrow took the acquisition legislation to the House, lawyers acting for Telemedia and the Ashcroft interests formally communicated that they would accept Government’s repudiation of the Accommodation Agreement and treat it as terminated — effectively arguing that Government could get rid of the infamous Agreement without taking away the company. Barrow proceeded with the acquisition anyway, maintaining that Belize’s problems with Ashcroft’s control of Telemedia went far beyond the Accommodation Agreement. Government acquired approximately 94% of Telemedia’s shares and related interests. By around this same time, three Ashcroft-linked companies — Heaver Holdings, Callerbar and Riddermark Ventures — held around 77.38% of Speednet.

In 2011, the Court of Appeal strikes down the Government’s takeover of BTL. Within weeks, Barrow’s UDP passed new acquisition legislation and subsequently enshrined Belizean majority ownership and control of BTL in the Eighth Amendment to the Belize Constitution. The next few years are filled with legal battles and arbitration in which firms associated with members of the Barrow family act as counsel for the Government of Belize, with substantial legal fees being paid along the way; but ultimately Belize forked over roughly $564 Million in nationalization-related compensation and settlement payments tied to the Ashcroft alliance.

Now, to rid BTL of the Ashcroft-linked majority ownership in Speednet for good, BTL could pay another near $100 Million if the deal closes on the disclosed terms. It is a feather in the cap of Belize’s pied piper. And shockingly, despite opposition from the unions, civil society and the Chamber of Commerce, the wider public response to the new Speednet acquisition has been remarkably muted. It is as if we are resigned or sensitized to the Ashcroft feeding frenzy. Are we simply too cynical, or disinterested to care? Perhaps the lack of response to this issue is because the current voting generation, were in school during the early 2000s and only vaguely heard of the BTL-saga but never knew the intricacies, or because the upcoming generation have never heard of the boogeyman Lord Michael Ashcroft. But the time to have taken a stand against the Speednet acquisition may already have passed. The BTL board has already voted to proceed, though the PUC review and final transaction documents remain outstanding, and approval seems imminent at this point. If the deal closes on the disclosed terms, this money must be paid by the end of 2030.

But thank the good Lord for the laughs and the memories! But is it he who indeed has the last laugh?

There is, however, another uncomfortable reality that deserves consideration: Belize may simply be too small a market to sustainably support two completely duplicated national telecommunications networks indefinitely. Competition sounds good in theory and has undoubtedly benefited consumers, but if two companies continuously cannibalize an already tiny market until neither generates enough profit to properly invest in infrastructure, the consequences are different when one of those companies is BTL. If SMART crumbles, its private shareholders lose. If BTL crumbles, Government loses, Social Security loses and ultimately the Belizean public loses. From the narrow financial perspective of BTL and the Social Security Board, therefore, acquiring SMART and eliminating duplicated operating costs may actually make business sense. The larger national question is what Belize replaces that competition with. If BTL becomes the single domestic national mobile operator, then Belize must ensure genuine outside competition remains possible — whether through Starlink, other international providers or future entrants — while the PUC must enforce prices, service standards, consumer protections, privacy and open access. The real danger may therefore not be the merger itself, but allowing a Government-controlled monopoly to emerge without strong enough competition and regulatory safeguards around it.

World.title: Police went searching the bushes and found seven little bricks waiting
World.content:
Police went searching the bushes and found seven little bricks waiting

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in Orange Walk have cleared yet another hidden stash spot, this time pulling seven small bricks of suspected crack cocaine from a bushy area along Naranjal Street during a late-night search, with no one around to claim them.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Friday, August 7, 2026, at about 11:00 p.m., members of the Quick Response Team attached to the Orange Walk Police Formation conducted a search of a bushy area on Naranjal Street.

During the search, an officer found a small transparent plastic containing seven small bricks of a buff substance suspected to be crack cocaine.

No one was in the immediate area at the time of the discovery, and the suspected drugs were taken to the Orange Walk Police Station as found property.

At the station, the suspected crack cocaine was weighed on a working digital gram scale, amounting to 4.3 grams. The drugs were placed in a labelled envelope and deposited as found property.

No arrests have been made, and the matter remains under police attention.

World.title: 18 year old bolts from station yard and stays free for six weeks before police find her
World.content:
18 year old bolts from station yard and stays free for six weeks before police find her

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A young woman who bolted from the compound of the Orange Walk Police Station moments after being brought in, outrunning pursuing officers into the night, has been recaptured nearly six weeks later and formally charged with escape from lawful custody.

According to the Belize Police Department, the saga began on Sunday, June 28, 2026, at approximately 11:45 p.m., when officers on mobile patrol along Maskal Street spotted a group of women sitting inside a park on the street. Officers approached and asked each individual for her name, and in doing so, one officer recognized a young woman who was wanted in connection with a cybercrime matter.

She was informed she would be detained and taken to the Orange Walk Police Station pending charges, and was escorted to the police mobile without incident. The compliance lasted exactly as far as the station yard. Upon arrival, she was instructed to exit the mobile, which she did, and while an officer was opening the other door, she ran out of the police station compound toward Democracia Street. Police gave chase, but she made good her escape into the night.

The trail stayed cold through July. Then, on Friday, August 7, 2026, she was detained once more, this time with no door left ajar. At the station she was read and issued her suspect’s rights in custody acknowledgement form, signing voluntarily, and was placed into custody pending charges.

In the early hours of Saturday, August 8, at 5:05 a.m., police obtained a warrant in the first instance and formally arrested and charged Kailyn Jacobs, an 18-year-old unemployed woman of Liberty Avenue, with the crime of escape from lawful custody.

It should also be noted that the cybercrime matter for which she was originally wanted remains exactly that in the report, a matter for which she was sought, with any charge on that front still to be confirmed.

Escape from lawful custody stands as its own offence regardless of the underlying matter, and Saturday’s charge carries its plain arithmetic: the June dash bought six weeks, and its price is now an additional count before the court that the original detention never carried.

World.title: Orange Walk parking lot fight proves saying “excuse me” can apparently get very expensive
World.content:
Orange Walk parking lot fight proves saying “excuse me” can apparently get very expensive

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Friday morning scuffle in an Orange Walk business parking lot has ended with both women involved formally charged with harm, after a confrontation that began with a shove and a request for basic courtesy left each with injuries certified by a doctor.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 23-year-old woman of San Pablo Village reported that on Friday, August 7, 2026, she and her sister were standing in a business parking lot eating meat pies when two women passed by, one of whom she has known for about two years.

According to the report, one of the women pushed herself between the two sisters, prompting the complainant to tell her to say excuse next time. The woman then turned around, came at them, pushed the sister out of the way, grabbed the complainant by her hair, and scratched her below the left eye. The complainant fought back, scratching the woman on both hands and her face. The sister jumped in and tried to separate the two but could not, and the complainant called her father, who brought her to the Orange Walk Police Station. Police brought the other women to the station as well.

At the station, both injured women were issued medico-legal forms, and a doctor certified both of their injuries as harm. Statements were recorded from both, and both were detained pending charges.

On Friday, August 7, police obtained a warrant in the first instance and formally arrested and charged both Angelina Gonzalez, a 23-year-old of San Pablo Village, and Merari Ramirez, a 27-year-old supervisor of Chan Pine Ridge Village, with the crime of harm. Both were cautioned and chose to remain silent, and both were granted bail to appear before the Magistrate Court on Monday, August 10, 2026, at 9:00 a.m.

On Monday morning, both sides of Friday’s parking lot quarrel will stand before the same magistrate, and the shove that started it all will be measured at its full price.

World.title: Boss sent employee on a sales run, but the pickup and cash ended up in Mexico
World.content:
Boss sent employee on a sales run, but the pickup and cash ended up in Mexico

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): An Orange Walk Town company is counting its losses after an employee sent out on a morning sales route failed to return with the company pickup or the cash he had collected, and immigration records confirm the man left Belize and entered Mexico that very day.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 50-year-old supervisor of a company operating in Orange Walk Town reported the matter on Thursday, August 6, 2026.

He told police that on Tuesday, August 4, at 8:00 a.m., an employee reported for duty at the company’s premises and was tasked to conduct sales within Orange Walk Town. The employee took the key and drove away in the company’s grey 2006 Nissan Frontier four-door pickup, valued at $20,000, approximately US$10,000, to commence his sales.

By about 6:30 p.m. that evening, the supervisor was informed by a colleague that the employee had not returned with either the company vehicle or the undisclosed amount of cash he had collected during the day. The supervisor further reported that company vehicles are for business use only, must be returned by 5:00 p.m. unless otherwise authorized, and are not permitted for personal use.

Police recorded a statement and circulated information to all border points, and the response settled the question of the man’s whereabouts: the northern border confirmed that the employee left Belize on August 4 and entered Mexico.

Several business places have been visited as part of the investigation, and a message for the man’s detention has been circulated to all police formations.

The border crossing places the case in increasingly familiar territory, joining a growing file of matters this season in which persons of interest have left the country as investigations opened, a pattern that tests the reach of Belizean officials and their cooperation with neighbouring states.

Anyone with information on the whereabouts of the company vehicle is asked to contact the Orange Walk police.

World.title: The weekend ends as it began: bright and hot
World.content:
The weekend ends as it began: bright and hot

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The weekend finishes the way it started, under sunshine. Mainly fair weather prevails across Belize this Sunday, with the familiar 95-degree inland heat, manageable seas, and one small twist: the northern districts may catch slightly more showers later today.

According to the National Meteorological Service, skies will be sunny with a few cloudy spells today and partly cloudy tonight. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated, with slightly more possible over the northern districts later today, a change of assignment from the south, which has carried the shower duty most of the week.

Temperatures along the coast will reach a high of 89 degrees Fahrenheit (32 Celsius) and a low of 83 (28 Celsius). Inland areas will climb to 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 Celsius) before dropping to 74 (23 Celsius). In the hills, expect a high of 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 Celsius) and a low of 68 (20 Celsius). The Sunday advice holds steady: water close, shade often, especially through the afternoon peak.

At sea, conditions run from a light chop to choppy, with easterly winds of 10 to 15 knots and waves of 2 to 5 feet, workable water for the weekend’s final boat runs with the usual care on smaller craft.

On the tropical front, the calm continues. Tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the region over the next 48 hours.

Looking ahead, Monday stays mainly fair with isolated showers or thunderstorms, before a few showers and thunderstorms may develop along the coast and some southern areas on Monday night, easing the country back into the working week.

Today’s high tides are at 6:11 AM and 8:32 PM, with a low tide at 2:10 PM and another low at 12:43 AM tomorrow. The sun rose at 5:34 AM and will set at 6:21 PM. The forecast was issued by forecaster Crystal Rosalez.

World.title: Two reportedly killed in fatal motorcycle collision on Mahogany Street
World.content:
Two reportedly killed in fatal motorcycle collision on Mahogany Street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Breaking Belize News has received reports of a serious traffic accident involving motorcycles on Mahogany Street in Belize City during the early hours of Sunday morning.

Preliminary information indicates that the accident occurred at around 2:00 a.m. and involved at least two motorcycles. Images from the scene show multiple persons on the roadway as bystanders and other individuals gathered nearby.

Initial reports indicate that at least one person may have died, while there are also unconfirmed reports suggesting that two persons were killed in the collision.

The identities of those involved and the circumstances leading to the accident have not yet been confirmed.

Breaking Belize News will provide additional information once an official report becomes available.

World.title: Teen drowns in Belize River after bee swarm attack
World.content:
Teen drowns in Belize River after bee swarm attack

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A quiet walk along the Philip Goldson Highway turned to tragedy on Friday, August 7, 2026, when a 17-year-old girl drowned in the Belize River after she and her father were attacked by a swarm of bees near mile 7, sending the teen into deep water from which she never resurfaced.

The attack came at about 1:00 p.m., as the girl and her father, residents of Lord’s Bank who often walked that route together, passed a tree stump where the bees were nesting. The swarm descended on them both, and in the chaos that followed, as passersby rushed to assist her father, the teen went into the river, likely to escape the stings. That stretch of the river is said to be about 20 feet deep, and the girl, who could not swim, was unable to get back to the surface.

What followed was an hours-long search that drew together the Belize Coast Guard and eight civilian volunteers from 501 Lifeguard, who waded and dove through dark, murky water until about 3:30 p.m., when her body was finally recovered.

Tevin Conorquie, the 501 Lifeguard swimming instructor who first located her, described the ordeal, speaking to local media. “All we could have done was free dive and try to scan the area,” he said. “Due to the darkness of the water, it was intense for us to see but we still pulled through, we had the faith and the courage and we did what we had to do.” The team spent some three to four hours in the water, in conditions Conorquie called very difficult, “due to the fact that we know there may be crocodiles with us as well.”

When the teen’s brother arrived and the loss became real, the rescuers’ work turned from search to solace, the 501 Lifeguard team circling him in prayer. “With our team it’s just love,” said the organization’s owner, Andrew Gentle, noting that his instructors left their swimming classes to answer the call, and the whole team came.

The recovery weighed on the professionals too. “It’s never easy because you’re talking about the loss of life,” said Rear Admiral Gregory Soberanis, Commandant of the Belize Coast Guard, which responded to the request for dive operations. “There were times when I myself shed tears because of the situation. Especially when you’re talking about a young person such as the one today.”

The girl’s father is currently recovering in hospital. The family shared that the teen was living with autism and resided with her father. Officials have since sprayed the area where the bees were nesting.

Breaking Belize News extends its deepest condolences to the family, and its gratitude to the divers and volunteers who refused to leave the river without her.

World.title: Bravery born of pain
World.content:
HIGGINS...I will do whatever I can to protect the kids of our society

FUELLED by her own childhood experiences with sexual assault and incidents of incest that she’d witnessed, Susan Higgins helped track down Troy Ellis, the man accused of the rape and murder of eight-year-old Talia Thompson in Discovery Bay, St Ann, in 2023.

Just shy of three years later, her actions have earned her national recognition. Higgins is among four Jamaicans slated to receive the Badge of Honour for Gallantry at this year’s national honours and awards ceremony scheduled for October.

Ellis, while receiving treatment at hospital under police guard following Talia’s death in September 2023, reportedly escaped. But Higgins later encountered him on the road and played a key role in getting him back into police custody.

For the 50-year-old, the national recognition is deeply personal.

“I feel happy and blessed to know that I can be a help to the helpless and a voice of the voiceless,” she told the

Jamaica Observer.

“When I opened the paper [last Thursday] and I saw Susan Higgins, mi dear! It was 140 people and fi mi name in there, me seh! No man, me feel good,” she added, erupting in laughter.

Talia was allegedly raped and murdered on September 23, 2023. Ellis, who was reportedly known to the family, was subsequently taken to hospital after allegedly injuring himself.

When Higgins heard that he had escaped from police custody, she said she immediately felt a sense of urgency to do something.

She said she was on her way home and her daughter was with her. When they got to the vicinity of the Firearm Licensing Authority office in Discovery Bay, she noticed a man attempting to conceal his face when the motor vehicle headlights illuminated him.

She said she immediately became suspicious and asked the driver to turn the vehicle around.

When they approached the man, Higgins said she began questioning him about his injury, deliberately remaining calm and acting as though she was simply curious about why he was on the road so late. She recalled Ellis telling her that he had recently been discharged from hospital.

Higgins said she continued to speak with him through the window of the vehicle while it drove slowly beside him, at the same time her daughter was conducting a quick online search. The search, she said, confirmed that the man she was speaking to matched the description of the escapee.

“I told him to pull up his shirt to let me see his wound. I was just playing slick because I wanted to see if he had a gun on him. When I saw that he didn’t have a gun, I asked him where he was going, and he said ‘Portland Road’,” she recalled.

“I said, ‘Do you need a ride?’ And he said, ‘Yes,’ not knowing it was the police me a carry him to. I said, ‘All right, when you reach your destination you tell me.’ During the ride, he was talking so intelligently to me. He didn’t show any sign of [being of] unsound mind, so I talked to him and talked to him until he said, ‘Me a come off here so.’ When he said that, me dumb, deaf, and blind, and stopped talking. I took him straight to Discovery Bay police,” said Higgins.

When they arrived, Higgins said the station’s door was closed, so she instructed her daughter to knock.

A cop came outside and Higgins said the driver immediately announced that they had found the man wanted in connection with Talia’s death. At that point, Higgins said Ellis became aware that he had been identified and attempted to resist.

She said she struggled to restrain him before eventually getting him into the police station, after which his identity was confirmed and he was returned to police custody.

For Higgins, the decision to intervene was not about recognition or praise, it was about doing what she would hope someone else would do if her child was in danger.

“Too many times children are being murdered, raped, left abandoned. As a woman, I didn’t get the love and the care of a parent. I actually grew up in the wild because my parents gave me away to a family, and [a man] attempted to rape me. It made me so aggressive, and I said if anybody ever do this to any pickney, if me catch them, me a go unalive them, but I did my best that night to not do what I wanted to because my little daughter was there and I couldn’t bear to do it,” she told the Sunday Observer.

“So many kids get raped and murdered, and so many of these cases go unanswered. I said, I am going to stand up and be a voice for the voiceless and a help for the helpless,” said Higgins.

“I will do whatever I can to protect the kids of our society,” she said. “I didn’t know the parents or the grandparents of that child, but I feel elated that I can help a mother to get some form of justice,” said Higgins.

“As I go along, I will always try to help somebody. My living will not be in vain,” she declared.

World.title: Running dry
World.content:
Paul Williams rinses a vehicle moments after it exited a drive-through car wash. (Photos: Naphtali Junior)

FACING the annual prospect of cutting staff or paying to truck untreated water just to keep their businesses afloat, car wash operators across Kingston and St Andrew say they are once again bracing for a difficult period as stricter restrictions loom.

Several operators told the Jamaica Observer they fear they may be forced to temporarily shutter their operation or find alternatives to clean vehicles if the drought persists, though many remain hopeful that rainfall will ease the situation before the restrictions intensify.

Last week, Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda warned that full prohibition orders on the use of potable water are possible by August 10, if weather conditions remain unchanged or worsen.

Samuda made the announcement after the Meteorological Service of Jamaica projected prolonged dry conditions stretching into October this year.

Under a prohibition order issued by the National Water Commission (NWC), the use of treated water for non-essential activities is banned during periods of severe drought. Prohibited activities include watering gardens, lawns and farms; refilling tanks, ponds and swimming pools; and washing vehicles with a hose. Breaches may result in a fine or imprisonment for up to 30 days.

Speaking at a Jamaica Observer Press Club earlier this year, Samuda said efforts are under way to strengthen the country’s water infrastructure, so Jamaica can avoid imposing similar restrictions during future dry spells. However, until then, restrictions will be in place.

David Chambers, manager of an auto spa, said he has worked in the industry for 30 years and is no stranger to water restrictions, describing them as one of the inevitable challenges the business faces whenever drought conditions arise.

He said the business typically copes by purchasing untreated water sourced from rivers. While the additional expense of trucking water significantly increases operating costs, Chambers said the auto spa absorbs the cost rather than passing it on to customers, fearing higher prices could drive away business.

“People have to still eat food, and the workmen have their families to feed, so it’s not a situation where we can just shut down the car wash. We have to find ways and means to operate,” he told the Sunday Observer.

He said that if trucked water is no longer available, he may have no choice but to close his business, a decision he would make with a heavy heart because of its impact on his employees. However, he said he is researching alternatives.

Chambers said he discovered waterless car-washing products that could allow the business to continue operating, but the specialised chemicals would have to be imported and come at a high cost, making the option difficult to sustain.

“Right now we are in a situation where we have to just watch and see what is happening more than anything else… We are praying for some rain because with rain we know that the water situation will go away because the [catchment] areas will have water, so that will be good for us,” said Chambers.

The cry for rain is also being made by Paul Williams, team leader at One Wash, a drive-thru car wash in the Corporate Area. Williams said currently, One Wash has three water drums on the premises which cost about $18,000 to refill. That will allow them to wash up to 20 cars.

“It affects us a lot, so we have to just try to wash off the cars fast. Luckily, the machine we use recycles water. We have a drum on the inside where it recycles, but for the machines that we use to rinse off the cars, we use the drum, and that takes water, so we try not to waste it,” said Williams.

“If it gets worse, we have to close until the water situation gets better. I’m not prepared for that. I have to go home and sit down and have no work. I don’t know how I am going to manage. I hope rain falls so we don’t have any more water restrictions because right now, I don’t have any water at my house. I got up this morning, and no water, and it’s going on two months now,” he told the Sunday Observer.

Williams appealed for improvement in Jamaica’s water resilience to ensure that businesses that rely on the supply do not have to close their doors.

“We need to find a fix. It cannot be that every year we have to lose business,” he argued.

Chenell Allison, a supervisor at Ten-O-Let Car and Carpet Care, said the company is often forced to make staff changes.

“We try to cut where we can, so maybe staff that is on weekly we give them fewer days,” Allison explained.

She added the company also has contractual workers who get paid per car, so it is less burdensome when business is slow and restrictions are in place.

Allison noted that the company currently trucks water to fill two tanks to stay afloat, but it cannot afford to do so for an extended period.

“If our budgeted amount for purchasing is exceeding profits, then we have a problem, but we are not there yet. We are used to it. It hasn’t come to that yet, so hopefully we can get some rain before it does and we have to shut down,” said Allison.

Another car wash operator said he does not believe it would be worth continuing the business if the drought worsens. He said he is prepared to conserve, because he has other businesses that are more profitable and do not require water usage.

He, too, called for measures to protect water-reliant businesses during a drought.

Samuda said the Government has several major projects under way aimed at making Jamaica more resilient during periods of drought. Among them is the Rio Cobre Water Treatment Plant, now under construction in Content, St Catherine, which he described as a game-changing investment.

The facility will treat raw water from Rio Cobre and inject 15 million gallons of potable water into the NWC’s distribution network each day, supplying more than 150,000 customers across St Catherine, Kingston and St Andrew. The project remains on track for completion in May 2027.

He said the Rio Cobre development forms part of a broader national strategy to strengthen Jamaica’s water infrastructure rather than relying on emergency measures whenever drought conditions arise. According to Samuda, investments made since 2015 have significantly improved water efficiency in Kingston, St Andrew and Portmore by reducing leakage across the network from 71 per cent to 37 per cent.
