Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector, despite Polish government measures to cushion the rise in consumer prices. Orlen has also this year seen its highest ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets. The results come amid a political dispute over a government plan to impose a windfall tax on excess profits from fuel sales, aimed at recouping billions spent on consumer subsidies. Orlen would be the biggest target of the tax, but the plan has been obstructed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. W pierwszym półroczu Orlen zarobił na czysto 15,8 miliarda złotych. Trzy razy więcej niż przed rokiem.https://t.co/qJS81csI0H — TVN24 BiS (@TVN24BiS) August 6, 2026 On Thursday, Orlen reported consolidated net profit of 15.9 billion zloty (€3.7 billion) for the first six months of the year, almost tripling from the 5.7 billion zloty recorded in the same period of 2025. Revenue rose to 152.2 billion zloty from 134.4 billion zloty. CEO Ireneusz Fąfara acknowledged that the figures came amid exceptional market conditions. Energy prices jumped globally in March, after the US and Israel began to attack Iran and Tehran responded by blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a key export route. Fąfara noted that, despite this, Poland had maintained some of Europe’s lowest fuel prices. He said that Orlen had prioritised fuel availability and competitive domestic prices while taking advantage of stronger margins abroad, where it brought in an “absolutely record level of revenue from foreign markets”. In the first half of 2026, foreign markets accounted for 35.7% of Orlen’s revenue, up from 33.8% a year earlier. The bulk came from Germany, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Austria, where Orlen operates petrol stations, as well as from trading activities in markets such as the Netherlands and Switzerland. Pierwsze półrocze 2026 roku ORLEN zamyka rekordowym zyskiem z rynków zagranicznych. Wynik netto całej Grupy w II kwartale wyniósł 7,7 mld zł. Wypracowane wyniki finansowe pozwoliły na wypłatę rekordowej dywidendy dla akcjonariuszy oraz dalsze finansowanie największego programu… pic.twitter.com/ohcxksuv4G — ORLEN (@GrupaORLEN) August 6, 2026 Orlen has expanded rapidly in recent years, as it has swallowed up other state-owned energy firms and sought to diversify away from its traditional focus on oil towards gas, renewables and hydrogen. In March this year, Orlen’s market valuation rose to its highest ever level of €35.2 billion, up from €7 billion in early 2022. As a result, it overtook the market capitalisation of Russian energy giant Gazprom. Mateusz Czyżkowski, an analyst at brokerage XTB, attributed Orlen’s record profits this year to “skilful balancing between geopolitical conditions and local pressures”, including government-imposed fuel price caps that squeezed margins. “The global commodities market in the second quarter of 2026 was strongly buoyed by tensions between Iran and Israel and ongoing disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz…This significant geopolitical premium boosted profits in [Orlen’s] Upstream & Supply segment,” he wrote in a note. The announcement of record profits comes as Orlen finds itself at the centre of a political dispute over the government’s proposed windfall tax, which would introduce a 60% levy on excess profits from liquid fuel sales. The measure was expected to raise around 4 billion zloty, which would have offset most of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by, among other things, cutting VAT and introducing a maximum daily price. However, although the tax was approved by the government’s majority in parliament in July, President Nawrocki refused to sign it into law, instead referring it to the constitutional court for review – a process that has no time limit and can take years. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 According to government calculations, Orlen would account for around 60% of the tax base if the measures eventually come into force. However, at his press conference on Thursday, Fąfara emphasised that the company supports the windfall tax. “We have viewed this solution positively from the very beginning. I believe it is in the interest of the company, our customers, and the country,” he said. However, Fąfara rejected suggestions that Orlen could unilaterally reduce pump prices by sacrificing margins. “We cannot lower prices in defiance of the market and global prices…If we lowered prices below parity, there would be a shortage of fuel,” he warned, adding that artificially low prices would encourage speculative exports and fuel tourism. Prices at petrol stations jumped today in Poland after the government ended the last of the support measures introduced to cushion consumers from the energy crisis caused by the war in Iran. Some places saw prices rise by as much as 14%https://t.co/mUfWUyDMle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2026 Prime Minister Donald Tusk used Orlen’s record profit announcement to reiterate criticism of the Nawrocki for obstructing the windfall tax. “Taxing such extraordinary profits made by oil companies, not just Orlen, was intended to bring down prices at petrol stations. That is precisely what Karol Nawrocki blocked. Remember this when you’re tanking up,” Tusk wrote on social media. Nawrocki’s office has, however, rejected the idea that an increased tax on fuel companies would somehow reduce fuel prices, arguing that, if anything, it would have the opposite effect if companies pass some of the costs onto consumers. Opodatkowanie takich nadzwyczajnych zysków koncernów paliwowych, nie tylko Orlenu, miały służyć obniżeniu cen na stacjach. New Polish opposition group Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which recently broke away from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, has proposed the idea of paying a “parental salary” for the first three years of a child’s life. The idea is part of a package of proposals to tackle Poland’s dire demographic situation released on Friday by Development Plus in its first major policy announcement since leader Mateusz Morawiecki announced that the group would soon become a political party. 3600 zł miesięcznie na dziecko do 3. roku życia – jedna z wielu propozycji @RozwojPlus dla demografii! Pensja Rodzicielska wynosząca równowartość płacy minimalnej, czyli obecnie około 3600 zł netto miesięcznie przez pierwsze 3 lata życia dziecka. To ponad czterokrotnie więcej… pic.twitter.com/253pwcskNK — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) August 7, 2026 The proposed parental salary would amount to 3,600 zloty (€837) per month, the equivalent of the minimum wage after taxes. It is 4.5 times more than the current child benefit payment of 800 zloty per month that all Polish parents of children under 18 receive. Development Plus says that the parental salary could be combined with income from other work that parents undertake and that it would include contributions towards their pensions. It would end once a child turns three, after which parents would have access to normal child benefit payments. The group says that, for now, the idea is just a proposal, based on expert analysis of how to tackle Poland’s demographic crisis, and that it now wants to “refine it through dialogue with Poles” rather than “imposing top-down provisions”. Poland has long been grappling with a shrinking, ageing population. Last year, the number of births fell to a new post-war low of 238,000, while deaths totalled 406,000. That marked the 13th consecutive year in which more people died than were born in Poland. The country’s fertility rate – meaning the average number of children that are born to a woman over her lifetime – fell to a new record low of 1.068 in 2025. That is one of the lowest figures anywhere in the world and well below the so-called “replacement rate” – the figure needed to ensure that the population does not decline – which is generally defined as 2.1. Poland’s fertility rate, already one of the lowest in the world, fell to a new record low of 1.07 in 2025, deepening concerns over the country's shrinking and ageing population https://t.co/OMGC1MpA5l — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Successive Polish governments have introduced various measures intended to boost the birth rate, though so far without clear success. The former PiS government, with Morawiecki as finance minister and later prime minister, introduced and expanded the current child benefit programme. While there was a brief bump in births after it was launched in 2016, numbers subsequently continued their downward trend. After PiS lost power in 2023, the current government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, continued the child benefit programme and also introduced new payments to support parents who return to work and restored funding for IVF treatment, which was previously cut by PiS. When announcing the proposed parental salary on Friday, Development Plus also outlined seven other proposed new policies to ease Poland’s demographic problems. One would allow workers to have a portion of their contributions go towards their parents’ pensions. Another pledged to provide better maternity care, including access to anaesthesia, a private hospital room and dedicated midwife, prenatal testing, and infertility treatment. Other policies promised more flexible working arrangements and mortgage repayments to prevent people from having to choose between a family or a career, as well as school hours and after-school care that “adapt to the lives of families, not the other way around”. Development Plus also proposed “granting parents the right to represent the voices of their minor children”. However, they provided no details of what this would mean in practice. Dzieci to nasza przyszłość! To fundament bezpieczeństwa Polski i polska racja stanu. Jak sprawić, by Polaków rodziło się coraz więcej? Oto strategia demograficzna dla Polski Stowarzyszenia @RozwojPlus🇵🇱➕. pic.twitter.com/1hiQPNuL47 — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) August 7, 2026 Development Plus was founded as an association by Morawiecki in April this year. That immediately prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. Matters came to a head last month, when PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński demanded that all the party’s lawmakers sign a pledge of loyalty and commit to leave any political associations they are part of. Morawiecki and his allies refused to do so, prompting Kaczyński to declare that meant they had effectively resigned from the party. Last week, Development Plus announced it had formed its own separate parliamentary caucus with 40 MPs in the Sejm, the most powerful lower house of parliament. The move immediately made it the third-largest group in the parliament, while also meaning PiS was no longer the biggest. On Monday this week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”, following PiS’s shift in a more hardline direction over recent months. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has called for Ukrainian men of conscription age who are not legally working to be deported to Ukraine. The policy, which continues a recent hardening of PiS’s position towards Ukraine and Ukrainians as it competes with the far right for support, was condemned by government figures, who called it “absurd” and “disgusting”. 🇵🇱 Bezpieczeństwo obywateli powinno być priorytetem każdego rządu. Potrzebne są zdecydowane działania wobec osób przebywających w Polsce niezgodnie z prawem. 👉 Udostępnij! 🔥 Ku nowemu rządowi! pic.twitter.com/m8MctmmPXd — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) August 6, 2026 On Thursday, PiS, which has recently been hit by falling support in the polls and the defection of a large breakaway group of more moderate MPs, held a policy convention at which it presented ideas it wants to implement if it returns to power after next year’s parliamentary elections. “One of [our] government’s first, most significant decisions will be to deport men, Ukrainians of military age, who are not legally working in Poland,” announced Tobiasz Bocheński, a deputy leader of the party. “They will have the opportunity to fight for their homeland, so that the horrors of this war can quickly end,” he continued. “Because for Central and Eastern Europe to be secure and free, Ukraine must win.” Bocheński denied that the policy was inhumane, noting that, in 2022, when PiS was in government, “Poles, like no other nation in Europe, opened their hearts, their homes and their wallets to women, children, the elderly and disabled people fleeing Putin’s bombs”. Poland was the primary destination for refugees fleeing Ukraine in 2022. Almost one million of them remain in the country, alongside hundreds of thousands of other Ukrainian immigrants, many of whom arrived before 2022. They are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group. In their announcement of the proposed policy, PiS gave no details of how it would work in practice, nor on what legal basis Ukrainians who are legally resident in Poland and have not violated any laws would be deported. News website Interia, which had reported on PiS’s plans shortly before they were officially announced, notes that data from Poland’s labour ministry show that only around 11,000 Ukrainians are registered as unemployed in Poland. The figures are not broken down by gender, but most are believed to be women. However, PiS’s policy would also apply to Ukrainians in the so-called grey economy, where people work informally without registering or paying taxes, reports Interia. Military-age Ukrainian men in other European countries should not receive social benefits, says Poland's foreign minister, @sikorskiradek. "There should be no financial incentives for avoiding the draft" https://t.co/5TcTqyDa6X — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2024 PiS’s plan was immediately criticised by government figures, with interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka calling it “an absurd idea” and “pure demagoguery”. She noted that over 95% of Ukrainian men of conscription age in Poland are working legally and paying taxes. “Without these people, many key sectors of the Polish economy would simply grind to a halt,” wrote Gałecka. “Stop the incitement.” Deputy interior minister Maciej Duszczyk, meanwhile, told broadcaster TVN that, among the Ukrainian men not working, many are wounded soldiers in Poland for treatment and rehabilitation or fathers caring for disabled children. Deportations are a “purely political, disgusting idea”, he added. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński wrote that, “when [PiS] was in power, they couldn’t even deport those who were breaking the law, and now they’re supposedly going to deport everyone without rhyme or reason”. Since taking power, the current government has increased deportations of foreigners who are in Poland illegally or broke the law while in the country. Last year, it carried out over 9,000 deportations, up from 7,200 in 2023, the last year that PiS was in power Absurdalny pomysł @pisorgpl ws. deportacji Ukraińców to czysta demagogia! Ponad 95% mężczyzn w wieku poborowym legalnie pracuje w 🇵🇱 i płaci podatki (dane ZUS).@OficjalnyJK zapowiada deportacje. A jak miałoby to wyglądać w praktyce? Patrole sprawdzające dokumenty na ulicach?… — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) August 6, 2026 During the conference on Thursday, PiS emphasised its tough approach to migration more broadly, saying that it would “create a new, restrictive system for foreigners” that would track each immigrant in the country. “Every foreigner will have their own individual account,” and if they commit any offences or fail to abide by any administrative obligations, “the information will be immediately entered into the system, and the deportation process will begin”, said Bocheński. “The only good migration is the return of Poles from abroad,” declared the party on social media. 🛡️ Bezpieczne granice to bezpieczna Polska. Skuteczna ochrona granic i walka z nielegalną imigracją to obowiązek każdego odpowiedzialnego państwa. 👉 Udostępnij! 🔥 Ku nowemu rządowi! pic.twitter.com/rRPZpmXi5U — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) August 6, 2026 In fact, it was during PiS’s time in power from 2015 to 2023 that Poland saw the largest wave of immigration in its history, and one of the largest anywhere in Europe. In every year between 2017 and 2022, Poland was the EU member state that issued the highest number of first residence permits to immigrants from outside the bloc. There are now over two million foreigners registered as living in Poland, making up just 5% of the population. Around three quarters are Ukrainians (1.55 million), with the next largest groups being Belarusians (139,300), Indians (26,100), Georgians (22,200), Russians (19,500), Vietnamese (15,100) and Turks (14,500). The number of foreigners with residence permits in Poland has reached two million, making up just over 5% of the country’s population, new government data show. The largest national group by far are Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians and Indians https://t.co/SI09WtR7hR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 26, 2026 While in government, PiS welcomed Ukrainian migrants and refugees and was a strong supporter of Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. However, since going into opposition, it has taken an increasingly tough line. That has reflected a broader shift in Polish society, with a variety of polls showing rising negative sentiment towards Ukraine and Ukrainians. Recent months have also seen a rise in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland, including a number of high-profile incidents. Meanwhile, two far-right parties that have long taken an anti-Ukrainian stance, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have soared in the polls, placing pressure on PiS to toughen its own position. One Confederation MEP, Stanisław Tyszka, mocked PiS’s latest policy announcement. “PiS wants to heroically deport hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians whom they themselves let into Poland,” he wrote. “Comedy.” The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s power grid operator, PSE, has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid an ongoing heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. However, following a meeting with PSE and other state energy officials, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has assured Poles that, despite “a very difficult period”, the “situation is under control” and power supplies are secure, thanks in part to the growth of renewables in recent years. ❗️PSE ponownie ogłaszają okresy przywołania na rynku mocy❗️ To już 3. raz w tym roku, kiedy operator sięga po to narzędzie. W historii zdarzyło się to tylko 5 razy, wliczywszy 3 przypadki tegoroczne, co pokazuje wyjątkowość roku 2026 dla energetyki. pic.twitter.com/DbCPnpyae4 — Jakub Wiech (@jakubwiech) August 6, 2026 PSE has called on contracted electricity generators to increase output and large consumers to cut use to help balance the grid on Thursday between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m., as temperatures have this week approached 40°C (104°F) in many parts of the country. The same measures were introduced on Tuesday, as the heatwave pushed up electricity consumption, partly due to increased use of air conditioning and refrigeration. Participants in Poland’s capacity market are paid for maintaining standby capacity and fulfilling their obligations when called upon by the operator. According to PSE, the mechanism is “a remedial measure” used when the generation capacity available to the operator falls significantly below the required safety level. Previously, the measures were invoked in June this year, amid another heatwave that saw Poland hit its highest-ever recorded temperature of 40.5°C. But before that, they had only been used twice since being introduced in 2018. Temperatures in Poland have reached the highest level on record, with a figure of 40.3°C (104.5°F) recorded this afternoon, as the heatwave that has hit Europe this week moves eastwards https://t.co/eRhRxiuCGq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 28, 2026 Poland’s weather institute IMGW issued heat warnings on Thursday for 13 of the country’s 16 provinces, with daytime temperatures forecast to reach between 33C and 38C. High temperatures and prolonged drought conditions have also pushed water levels in many rivers to extremely low levels, with the Vistula, Poland’s longest river, only 5 centimetres above the historic low of 4 centimetres it fell to in Warsaw last year. Some other parts of the river have hit all-time record lows, reports Polsat News. One result has been a disruption of cooling supplies to Poland’s power sector. State energy firm Enea this week announced reduced operations at two of its coal-fired plants that are cooled by water from the Vistula. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity (just over 1% of Poland’s total) has gone offline. On Wednesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk convened a meeting of a government crisis team, including PSE’s deputy president, to discuss the current heatwave and its potential impact on the power sector. However, afterwards he assured that “the situation is under control” and that the fact that Poland now has “a lot of energy from solar panels and wind turbines makes our system relatively secure”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland’s renewable sector has expanded rapidly over the last decade. Last year, it provided just over 29% of the country’s power, with onshore wind supplying 14% of the energy mix and solar 12%. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. World.title: Polish top court confirms withholding funds from opposition PiS party over campaign finance irregularities
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s top administrative court has upheld a decision by the finance ministry to withhold state subsidies from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party due to campaign finance irregularities. The decision was welcomed by the government, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying that there will be “no money for grifters”. PiS, however, argues that the money is being withheld for political reasons and accuses the authorities of “Russian standards”. Naczelny Sąd Administracyjny oddalił w środę kasacje ws. dotacji i subwencji dla PiS. – Miażdżący dla PiS wyrok podtrzymany! – stwierdził szef MF Andrzej Domański https://t.co/bcL18WbiYf — OKO.press (@oko_press) August 6, 2026 The dispute dates back to August 2024, when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected PiS’s financial report for the previous year’s parliamentary election campaign after identifying around 3.6 million zloty (€838,000) in unauthorised expenditure. As a result, the PKW ordered that PiS should lose 10.8 million zloty from the state subsidies that political parties in Poland receive based on their level of electoral support. The party would normally have received 25.9 million zloty based on its 2023 election result. The decision triggered months of legal wrangling, with PiS arguing that the funding should be restored after the Supreme Court upheld its complaint against the PKW’s decision. However, finance minister Andrzej Domański refused to release the money, saying there were unresolved legal doubts over the ruling. The finance minister has refused to comply with the electoral commission's decision to pay out subsidies to the opposition PiS party He says there are "legal doubts" over the issue. But PiS says he is obliged to pay and will be held criminally responsible https://t.co/ZwIZRqn5tp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2025 Those doubts stem from a broader dispute over the controversial and contested judicial reforms implemented by PiS when it ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023. The chamber of the Supreme Court that ruled in PiS’s favour was created as part of those reforms. It has previously been found to not be a legitimate body by both the European Court of Justice and European Court of Human Rights because it contains improperly appointed judges. After the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling, the PKW initially said it would not recognise the decision until the chamber’s legal status was clarified. Two weeks later, however, it reversed that decision and approved PiS’s financial report. Domański still declined to restore the subsidy, arguing that the PKW’s resolution was internally contradictory. While it approved the payments, it also stated that the chamber’s ruling should come from a body recognised as a court and that it was not determining whether the chamber met that standard. PiS challenged Domański’s decision. However, its case was initially rejected by a lower court in June last year, and that decision has now been upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), which is the final court of appeal for administrative issues. The NSA found the minister had acted lawfully in withholding the funding. It also said the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling had no legal effect because it had been issued by a body that was not a properly constituted court, reports news website OKO.press. The ruling was welcomed by Domański, who called it a “crushing blow to PiS” and said that “yet another PiS lie has been exposed”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk, meanwhile, wrote on social media: “Just as we said, there is and will be no money for grifters.” Tak jak mówiliśmy, dla przekręciarzy pieniędzy nie ma i nie będzie. https://t.co/4Kqexj6NoC — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 5, 2026 The PKW’s decision to cut PiS’s funds was made after it found that government resources – including from the justice ministry, Government Legislation Centre (RCL) and Research and Academic Computer Network (NASK) – had been used to support the party’s election campaign. However, PiS has always argued that the decision was a political one, implemented at the behest of the new Tusk government in order to undermine the main opposition party. Radosław Fogiel, a senior PiS lawmaker and former party spokesman, said that the new NSA ruling “does not change the essence of the matter: it unlawfully deprives the main opposition party of the subsidy to which it is entitled. Russian standards.” Chłopie, powstrzymaj emocje! Ekscytacja jak u nastolatka przed pierwszą randką. A czego dotyczy ów "miażdżący wyrok"? Skargi na bezczynność Ministra Finansów. After a ten-year-long investigation, prosecutors have concluded that Poland’s government in 2010 – which was led by current Prime Minister Donald Tusk – was not guilty of “diplomatic treason” in its response to the plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party – which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023 and is led by Lech’s twin brother, Jarosław – has always rejected the findings of official Polish and Russian investigations into the crash, which found it to have been an accident. Instead, PiS claims that the disaster, which claimed the lives of 96 people, many of them senior Polish state officials, was caused deliberately by Russia and then covered up with the help of Tusk’s government. However, while PiS launched various investigations during its time in power, it has never substantiated its claims. And prosecutors now say that there is no evidence that diplomatic treason, a crime that carries a potential prison sentence of up to ten years, took place. Uprzednio wygrałem sprawę cywilną z posłem @OficjalnyJK, który w efekcie musiał wpłacić 50,000zł na siły zbrojne broniącej się Ukrainy. Teraz potwierdzenie @PK_GOV_PL: nie było żadnej zdrady dyplomatycznej ani żadnej intencji jej popełnienia. Oczywiście żaden z kłamców… https://t.co/VKZHlF5xkX — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 5, 2026 Wednesday’s announcement by the National Prosecutor’s Office was welcomed by Radosław Sikorski, the current foreign minister, who held the same role in 2010. He condemned the “Smolensk liars”, such as Jarosław Kaczyński, who he suggested had exploited the tragedy for their own benefit. “They brainwashed millions of people, divided families, stirred up hatred within the nation,” he wrote. “They’ll burn in hell for it. But the power, money and satisfaction they gained from spitting on their rivals – that’s theirs.” The idea that Smolensk was an assassination of Lech Kaczyński has been a core part of PiS rhetoric. In 2022, for example, Jarosław Kaczyński said that the decision was made “at the highest level of the Kremlin” and Tusk’s government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”. Smolensk was an “attack decided at the highest level of the Kremlin”, says Jarosław Kaczyński ahead of the 12th anniversary of the crash. Donald Tusk's government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”, he adds https://t.co/5ae0gHJj3B — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 4, 2022 The investigation into diplomatic treason – a crime consisting of acting to the detriment of Poland while authorised to represent the country in relations with foreign states or organisations – was launched in August 2016, less than a year after PiS had come to power. Among the individuals who had formally notified prosecutors of a potential crime was PiS deputy leader Antoni Macierewicz, who from 2015 to 2018 served as defence minister. He has been the foremost proponent of conspiracy theories around the Smolensk air disaster. In their notifications to prosecutors, Macierewicz and the others accused Tusk and other officials of, in their relations with Russia, deliberately choosing a legal basis for an investigation into the crash that was unfavourable to Poland by giving it no real influence over how it was run. However, prosecutors now say that, after ten years in which they questioned 488 witnesses, gathered extensive documentation and requested legal assistance from several countries, they have “concluded that no crime of diplomatic treason was committed”. In a statement explaining the decision, the National Prosecutor’s Office said that the legal basis chosen for cooperating with Russia on an investigation – Annex 13 of the Convention on International Civil Aviation – was, in fact, “the most advantageous solution” for Poland. It ensured the participation of Polish representatives in the Russian-led investigation, including access to the wreckage and crash site. Other legal options would have offered no greater benefits and involved significant risks, concluded the Polish prosecutors. They acknowledged that Russia “subsequently failed to fulfil some of its obligations arising from the adopted procedure”, but said this should have no bearing on assessing the decisions that were previously made on setting up the investigation. The defence ministry will notify prosecutors of 41 suspected crimes linked to a commission established by the former PiS government to investigate the 2010 plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński https://t.co/aEAlmk9lDM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2024 The prosecutors also found that, not only did Polish officials choose the best legal solution, but there was also “no evidence indicating that individuals authorised to act on behalf of Poland, including the prime minister and members of the Council of Ministers, acted with the intent to harm Poland”. Given that the crime of diplomatic treason requires intent, this finding further reinforced the decision to drop the investigation. However, the prosecutors note that their decision can still be appealed. At the time of writing, neither Kaczyński, Macierewicz, nor other senior PiS figures had commented on the prosecutors’ announcement. However, it is likely they will point to the fact that the current national prosecutor was appointed by Tusk’s government after it had removed the previous PiS-era incumbent in a legally questionable move. The Supreme Court has issued a ruling that effectively found that the government unlawfully replaced a senior prosecutor earlier this year However, the justice minister says the ruling has no legal force as it was issued by illegitimately appointed judges https://t.co/9fCE6d18uy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 27, 2024 In 2020, in a separate civil case, a court ordered Jarosław Kaczyński to apologise for accusing Sikorski of “diplomatic treason” in relation to the Smolensk crash. Two years later, after Kaczyński had refused to comply with the ruling and Sikorski published the apology himself, Kaczyński was ordered to pay the costs. In 2024, an investigation by Tusk’s government found that the PiS administration had wasted tens of millions of zloty on a commission, headed by Macierewicz, that was tasked with re-investigating the Smolensk disaster. It notified prosecutors of dozens of suspected crimes relating to the functioning of the commission. Macierewicz, however, accused the government of spreading “lies and disinformation” designed to “protect Putin”. Jarosław Kaczyński has been ordered to pay 700,000 zl (€150,000) to publish an apology to ex-foreign minister @sikorskiradek. Kaczyński has yet to comply with a 2020 order to apologise for accusing Sikorski of "treason" in relation to the Smolensk crash https://t.co/o0XkTWFgDR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2022 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Where to See the Partial Solar Eclipse in Prague and Across Czechia
World.content:
Skywatchers in the Czech Republic will have two reasons to look up on the night of August 12.

A partial solar eclipse will be visible in the evening, followed by favorable conditions for watching the annual Perseid meteor shower.

The eclipse will be visible across Czechia shortly before sunset, with the Sun low over the western and northwestern horizon. In Prague, the partial eclipse is expected to begin at about 7:19 p.m., reach its maximum at 8:12 p.m. and end around 8:27 p.m.



At the height of the eclipse, the Moon will cover about 86 percent of the Sun’s disk in Prague, making the event particularly noticeable if skies are clear.

The eclipse will look different depending on where observers are located. The farther east they are, the later the eclipse will begin and the less of it will be visible. In eastern Czechia and much of Slovakia, the maximum phase will take place after sunset, when the Sun is already below the horizon.

The event will be a partial eclipse in Central Europe, while a total solar eclipse will be visible in parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain. Astronomers and eclipse enthusiasts are expected to travel to those areas to experience totality.

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, blocking part or all of the Sun from view. In Czechia, the eclipse will be especially low on the horizon, so observers will need an unobstructed view toward the west and northwest.

Several Czech observatories are preparing public observing events. A list of locations and other information about the eclipse is available through the Czech astronomical website astro.cz.

Perseid meteor shower will follow

The same night will also offer good conditions for watching the Perseids, one of the most prominent annual meteor showers.

The shower will reach its peak during the early hours of August 13, when the Moon will be only a few hours past its new-moon phase. With virtually no moonlight in the sky, faint meteors should be easier to spot.

The Perseids are active from July 17 through August 24, but the best opportunity this year will come during the night of August 12-13.

Under dark skies and favorable weather, observers away from cities could see between 50 and 80 meteors per hour.

Light pollution will be the main obstacle for anyone hoping to see large numbers of meteors. The best locations are well away from major cities, ideally several dozen kilometers from strong sources of artificial light.

World.title: Non-Alcoholic Beer Sales Rise by More Than 25% in Czechia
World.content:
Beer remains a staple of the Czech shopping basket, but new sales data from online supermarket Rohlík shows that drinking habits are gradually changing.

Traditional lagers still dominate, while non-alcoholic beer is recording the fastest growth among the main beer categories.

The category has grown by more than a quarter over the past year, with Birell among the brands driving the increase. Birell sales alone are up by almost 20%.



Together with flavoured beers and radlers, non-alcoholic beer now accounts for close to one-third of all beer sales on Rohlík.

Beer from small and regional breweries is also gaining ground, with sales increasing by more than 11%.

The biggest decline is being recorded among craft beers grouped by style, including IPA and APA. This is currently the only major beer segment experiencing a year-on-year drop.

Czech brands continue to dominate the market. More than nine out of every 10 beers sold through Rohlík are from domestic brands.

Imported beers, however, are growing at a faster rate. Their sales have increased by 18% year-on-year.

Beer sales peak at the weekend

Friday is the busiest day for beer sales, with roughly twice as much beer sold as on Monday. Friday and Saturday together account for almost two-fifths of the category’s weekly sales.

Orders containing beer also tend to include significantly more items than orders without beer, suggesting that customers often buy it as part of a larger meal or weekend shop rather than as a standalone purchase.

Seasonal patterns have also shifted. Beer sales during this year’s summer months have reached levels comparable with the December Christmas peak.

World.title: Explore Holašovice: A UNESCO-Listed Gem with Its Own Stonehenge
World.content:
For over 20 years, the South Bohemian village of Holašovice has held a place on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

Located approximately 16 kilometers west of České Budějovice, this village is famed for its picturesque houses, built in the distinctive Peasant Baroque style.



The first recorded mention of Holašovice dates back to the late 13th century. The village has a rich and storied history, marked by events such as the Hussite wars and a devastating plague in the 16th century that significantly reduced the local population.

The iconic houses that now define Holašovice were constructed in the latter half of the 19th century, reflecting the Baroque, Rococo, and Classical influences prevalent in South Bohemian architecture of that era.

The village’s ethnic composition underwent significant changes during and after World War II. Following the establishment of the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, the Czech residents were forced to leave Holašovice, and the village was annexed to the Third Reich.

After the war, the German population was expelled, once again altering the village’s demographics.

Lada’s Pond and the Czech Stonehenge

Despite its turbulent past, Holašovice has retained a unique atmosphere that continues to attract visitors.

In addition to its charming houses, tourists can explore the local chapel and the picturesque Lada’s Pond, which, along with a statue of a water sprite, seems to be straight out of a painting by Josef Lada.

Just outside the village lies a unique stone circle, often referred to as the “Czech Stonehenge.” This site was designed to channel negative energy away from the human body, offering visitors a chance to experience its reputed healing properties.

World.title: Prague 7 Plans Floating Swimming Pool on the Vltava in Holešovice
World.content:
A floating swimming pool could be built along the Vltava River in Prague’s Holešovice district, near U Vody Park.

Prague 7 City Hall is considering using a section of the waterfront near the Port 7 development for the project.

The municipality hopes the pool could be ready within three years, although the cost has not yet been determined.

The project is still in its early stages. The district is currently looking into whether it could obtain older or unused pontoons and adapt them to create the swimming facility.



One of the main questions is where the pool water would come from. Prague 7 is considering both the Vltava and the municipal water supply.

The aim would be to use this data to determine when swimming in the river is considered safe. Čižinský has suggested introducing a simple traffic-light system similar to those used in cities such as Copenhagen and Amsterdam, allowing swimmers to see whether conditions are suitable.

According to Čižinský, the Vltava generally has good enough water quality for swimming, although conditions can deteriorate after heavy rainfall.

Recent measurements support this concern. Prague hygiene officials have been monitoring the water at Branická beach since the beginning of this year. The water has generally received a rating of two on the five-level scale used by hygienists.

The Holešovice proposal is not the first plan to introduce a floating swimming facility on the Vltava.

A similar idea was included in an earlier proposal to transform Prague’s riverfront. The project near Vyšehrad envisaged a large floating structure measuring 69 by 7.5 meters, with a swimming pool and a smaller paddling pool. A second connected vessel would have provided facilities for visitors.

The proposal was later put aside. In 2025, Prague property councilor Adam Zábranský of the Pirates said the investment was not among the city’s priorities.

World.title: Construction Disrupts Prague Tourists and Businesses During Peak Summer Season
World.content:
Construction projects across Prague’s historic center are proving a pain for tourists and locals alike who say the clumps of dirt, building supplies and equipment block popular sites and make it difficult to move around one of Europe’s most visited cities.



Heading down Národní to the Charles Bridge or going for a beer near the Vltava river now looks more like a vast construction site where tourists need to look out for more than the cobble-stone streets and baroque spires.

“It’s their first time here too, [they’ve] never seen it and now it’s torn up,” said Sherryl, a tourist visiting from the United States with her friends.

A major source of the disruption are upgrades to the public transport system. The central tram route delivering travelers to the heart of the city near the Národní Divadlo stop has been shuttered for weeks.

The disruption has taken a heavy toll on surrounding businesses like Aggeo, an Italian grocery store along the corridor. Its manager, Irena Kumpová, noted a sharp drop in foot traffic from travelers and regular local customers, who stroll by the National Theater on their way to gaze at the artist David Černý’s famous Kafka head.

“I’d rather stay closed… it’s a catastrophe,” remarked Kumpová.

With tourism growing every year in Prague, the widespread construction is making its mark this summer. So far this year, 1.7 million people have visited Prague, marking the strongest start in 15 years, according to Prague City Tourism and the Czech Statistical Office.

Tram services are suspended through the city center, clogging the streets and forcing many to find another way to work or home. For businesses that rely on heavy foot traffic during the busiest months of the year, that means less earnings.

“I have a table outside, but mainly just to signal to people that we’re open, but no one sits there right now,” said Kumpová.

The reconstruction is part of Prague’s broader effort to modernize its transport network, including long-term investments such as the future tram connection to Wenceslas Square and the expansion of Metro Line D as the city seeks to expand public transport.

Not everybody minds the disruption. The loud machines, dusty air, and obstructed sidewalks offer a certain charm for some who view the construction as part of the sightseeing experience.

“Despite the construction, it’s still beautiful,” said Raluca Costachescu, a traveler from Romania.

Written by: Mae Bryant, Bilyana Spasova, Milica Petrušová, Zuzana Kormančíková, Zhanna Bekiryan

World.title: Live Nation and PPF to Run Three Major Prague Venues
World.content:
Live Nation and PPF Group are forming a joint venture that will operate three of Prague’s major event venues — O2 Arena, O2 Universum and Forum Karlín.

The companies plan to invest in the venues and upgrade their facilities, with Live Nation set to hold a 51 percent stake in the new company.

The agreement will bring together one of the world’s largest live entertainment companies and PPF, the investment group that owns O2 Arena and O2 Universum through its subsidiary Bestsport.



PPF has also operated Forum Karlín, which has been owned by Patria Investment Company since last year.

The companies announced the planned partnership in a joint statement. Financial details of the transaction and the amount of the planned investment have not been disclosed. The deal remains subject to the required regulatory approvals.

Under the agreement, the new operator will be responsible for the day-to-day running of all three venues, including event planning and programming. The venues themselves will remain under their existing ownership structures, and their names will not change.

The partners said they intend to invest substantially in the facilities over the coming years. The aim is to improve conditions for audiences and performers while expanding the number of events held in Prague and strengthening the city’s position on the international concert and entertainment circuit.

PPF said the cooperation with Live Nation is also part of its strategy of developing the long-term value of its assets alongside major international companies.

Live Nation Entertainment operates across several areas of the live entertainment industry, including concert promotion, ticketing and sponsorship. Its businesses include Live Nation Concerts, Ticketmaster and Live Nation Sponsorship.

PPF Group is an international investment company with holdings across Europe, North America and Asia. Its portfolio includes telecommunications, media, financial services, real estate, e-commerce, industry and biotechnology.

World.title: Prague to Restore Tram Service Between Holešovice and City Center
World.content:
Residents of Prague 7 will regain a tram connection between Holešovice and the city center from September, with tram line 5 set to operate through the district and continue toward Wenceslas Square.

The change follows months of pressure from Prague 7 officials and local residents, who have called for better tram connections since the cancellation of line 14.

The district had previously requested either the return of line 14 or the introduction of an equivalent service and organized a petition supporting the demand.



The new arrangement will initially be temporary. According to the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) system, two trams will operate on the route at least through December 2026.

Line 5 to replace temporary route

The new service is linked to planned transport changes in Žižkov. Because of a traffic closure there, tram line 34 will be replaced by line 5 in Holešovice.

At Holešovice train station, line 5 will connect with line 6, effectively creating a continuous service between the two routes. Trams will run from the station through the Holešovice area, past the market and across Vltavská Street before continuing toward Wenceslas Square and other parts of central Prague.

For passengers in Holešovice, the move restores a connection that was lost when line 14 was discontinued.

Service could change again next year

The situation between January and June 2027 has not yet been fully settled. According to PID, the final arrangement will depend in part on discussions between the incoming leaderships of Prague 3 and Prague 7.

Maintaining the additional tram service in Holešovice during that period could require limited reductions elsewhere in Prague 3. Another option would be to temporarily return to the existing arrangement using combined tram lines 6 and 34.

PID has warned that permanently combining lines 5 and 6 could also create delays at both ends of the route. Such a change could affect passengers travelling through Prague 2 and Prague 5, even though it would provide the direct connection sought by Prague 7.

World.title: “Ivan, Go Home!” Rally to Take Place Outside Russian Embassy in Prague
World.content:
A Czech-Ukrainian rally will take place outside the Russian Embassy in Prague on August 20 to mark the 58th anniversary of the Soviet-led invasion of Czechoslovakia.

The event, titled “Ivan, Go Home!”, is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. on Thursday, August 20, at Boris Němcova Square in Prague 6.

The rally comes one day before the anniversary of the night of August 20-21, 1968, when troops from five Warsaw Pact countries entered Czechoslovakia to crush the Prague Spring reform movement.



The invasion brought an end to the country’s attempt to pursue a more liberal form of socialism and was followed by two decades of political repression and Soviet military presence.

The event is being organized jointly by People in Need (Člověk v tísni), Memory of the People (Paměť národa), Million Moments for Democracy (Milion chvilek pro demokracii), and the European Congress of Ukrainians.

Organizers say the rally will connect the historical experience of the Soviet occupation with Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Participants will gather to remember those killed or persecuted following the 1968 invasion and the people who lived under the communist regime that followed. The organizers also plan to express support for Ukraine and draw attention to what they describe as the continuing use of imperial violence by Russia.

The choice of the rally’s name refers to one of the best-known slogans associated with the 1968 invasion. “Ivan, go home!” appeared on posters, walls, buildings and military vehicles as Czechoslovaks protested against the foreign troops occupying the country.

The invasion halted those reforms. Soviet troops remained in Czechoslovakia until the end of the communist era, while the subsequent period of “normalization” brought censorship, political purges and restrictions on civil liberties.

World.title: Ferencváros narrowly beaten by Real Madrid at packed Groupama Arena
World.content:
Ferencváros suffered a narrow 2-1 defeat to Real Madrid in a high-profile friendly at Budapest’s Groupama Arena on Saturday, but the Hungarian champions gave their illustrious opponents plenty to think about and found the net through Kenan Kodro.

Fradi impress against European giants

Real Madrid took control late in the first half when Mario Rivas headed the visitors in front, before Carlos Espí doubled their advantage shortly after the interval. Ferencváros responded through Kodro in the 57th minute and grew into the game, but could not find the equaliser.

The result nevertheless represented a memorable occasion for Ferencváros, who welcomed one of football’s most decorated clubs to their home ground.

Groupama Arena turns white and green

The match attracted an unusually large number of Real Madrid supporters, with fans wearing shirts bearing the names of stars such as Federico Valverde, Jude Bellingham, Kylian Mbappé, Vinícius Júnior and Rodrygo.

Inside the stadium, Real Madrid shirts were considerably more prominent than usual alongside Ferencváros’ traditional green-and-white colours.

On the pitch, however, the colours were reversed. Ferencváros wore a new pale-gold and off-white kit, while Real Madrid appeared in green. The atmosphere was lively from the start, with the stadium filling rapidly before kick-off.

Real Madrid dominate but Fradi stand firm

Ferencváros did not appear intimidated by their illustrious opponents and created several promising attacks in the opening stages, although their efforts failed to seriously trouble the Madrid goal.

As the first half progressed, Real increasingly controlled possession. Their quick passing and explosive movement forced Ferencváros deeper, with the visitors repeatedly attempting shots from distance.

The hosts’ first major defensive test came in the 36th minute, when Endrick found space in the area, only for goalkeeper Dénes Dibusz to keep out his close-range effort.

Real’s pressure finally produced a goal in the 41st minute. Arda Güler’s corner reached Alexis Ciria, who returned the ball into the danger area, allowing Mario Rivas to head Madrid into the lead.

Madrid’s stars make their mark

The second half brought a major change in personnel for the Spanish giants, with Vinícius Júnior, Dean Huijsen, Antonio Rüdiger, Trent Alexander-Arnold, Carlos Espí and Bernardo Silva among those introduced.

The arrival of several established stars immediately increased Madrid’s attacking threat. After an impressive passing move, Federico Valverde provided the final pass for Carlos Espí, who finished calmly to make it 2-0.

Ferencváros responded quickly. In the 57th minute, Kristoffer Zachariassen delivered an excellent cross from the right, and Kenan Kodro met it at the near post to fire the ball into the bottom-left corner. The Groupama Arena erupted, with even some Real Madrid supporters applauding the home side’s goal.

Fradi push for an equaliser

The goal changed the complexion of the match. Ferencváros began escaping the pressure that had characterised much of the first half and regularly worked their way towards Madrid’s penalty area.

Zachariassen came close again with a header, but his effort went straight into the hands of goalkeeper Andriy Lunin.

Real continued to threaten from set pieces, with Trent Alexander-Arnold, Federico Valverde and Güler among those around a late free-kick. Güler ultimately sent his effort over the crossbar.

As the final whistle approached, Ferencváros looked capable of finding an equaliser, with the flow of the game suggesting they were closer to making it 2-2 than Real were to extending their lead. The second goal ultimately failed to arrive.

Encouraging test ahead of European football

Real Madrid therefore left Budapest with a 2-1 victory, but Ferencváros can take considerable encouragement from their performance.

The Hungarian side competed well against one of the world’s biggest clubs, absorbed sustained pressure, scored against Madrid after the interval and created chances to level the match.

The friendly was nevertheless only part of a busy summer schedule. Ferencváros’ attention now turns to the return leg against Górnik Zabrze in Europa League qualifying.

That fixture will carry far greater competitive importance, but after their performance against Real Madrid, Fradi can approach it with plenty of confidence.

World.title: ‘We were told what was good for us’: Hungarian minister vows to change attitudes towards disabled people
World.content:
Ensuring physical and digital accessibility “is my pet project”, the minister of social and family affairs said on Facebook on Sunday, after receiving visually impaired guests from south-eastern Hungary’s Békés county at his ministry.

In his post, the minister slammed the previous government by saying that people living with a handicap “were not in the focus” in the past 16 years.

“Accessibility and equal opportunities were strongly suppressed; we were paternalised and told what was good for us,” the minister, who is visually impaired himself, said. He added he would work to change those attitudes and asked civil organisations to signal problems.

Meanwhile, Kátai-Németh said it was crucial to provide jobs for the handicapped.

World.title: Transylvanian villagers attack ambulance after seeing TikTok rumours about kidnapping children
World.content:
An ambulance crew was attacked with stones, sticks and axes in a Transylvanian village after residents reportedly mistook the emergency vehicle for one allegedly linked to an online kidnapping rumour.

Angry Transylvanian villagers attack emergency vehicle with stones, sticks and axes

The incident took place on Saturday evening in Recea-Cristur, a village in Transylvania region’s Cluj County around 40 kilometres from the city of Dej.

Romania’s Health Ministry said on Sunday that the ambulance was attacked amid unfounded rumours circulating on TikTok about so-called “black ambulances” allegedly being used by organ traffickers to abduct children. The ambulance driver suffered a serious eye injury during the attack.

Ambulance blocked by two cars

The Cluj County Ambulance Service vehicle had travelled to Recea-Cristur to collect a patient. According to the accounts cited by Romanian authorities, the crew encountered hostility as soon as they arrived in the village. Residents reportedly filmed the ambulance on their mobile phones while the crew was trying to find the patient’s address.

The situation escalated when two cars were allegedly used to block the ambulance in the centre of the Transylvanian village, forcing the vehicle to stop. Several people then reportedly attacked the ambulance using stones, sticks and axes.

The emergency crew’s doctor said they may have faced an even more serious situation had the driver not managed to turn the ambulance around and escape in the opposite direction.

Romanian ambulance vehicle. Illustration. Featured image: depositphotos.com

Driver taken to operating theatre

After the crew reached hospital in Dej, the ambulance driver also required medical treatment. A fragment of the vehicle’s shattered windscreen reportedly struck the driver’s eye and injured the cornea. The driver subsequently underwent surgery.

The incident has highlighted the potentially serious consequences of rumours targeting emergency services, particularly when false claims spread rapidly through social-media platforms.

Authorities link attack to TikTok rumours

Police said the attack in Transylvania was connected to unfounded rumours circulating on TikTok claiming that organ traffickers were travelling around Romanian communities in ambulances in order to abduct children.

Romanian authorities have repeatedly rejected the claims and urged the public to rely on verified information from official sources rather than unconfirmed social-media posts.

The Romanian Interior Ministry issued another warning on Sunday, publishing screenshots of three TikTok posts promoting claims about the so-called “black ambulance”.

According to the ministry, photographs used in the posts as supposed “warnings” had been manipulated or generated using artificial intelligence.

Never miss a headline: join our newly-launched Messenger group!

Authorities: no recorded case of an ambulance being used for kidnapping

In its warning, Romania’s Interior Ministry said that the country had never recorded a case in which an ambulance was used to abduct people.

The ministry stressed that ambulances are operated by medical professionals whose role is to save lives, and warned that misinformation can have consequences beyond simply causing public anxiety.

False rumours, it said, can place emergency workers in danger when they are responding to calls for help. The authorities therefore urged members of the public not to share alarming claims without checking their authenticity.

More on the region: Hungarian journalist attacked by bear near Fidesz’s annual Transylvanian festival

Misinformation puts emergency workers at risk

For ambulance crews, reaching a patient quickly can be a matter of life and death. Any attempt to block an emergency vehicle, intimidate its crew or prevent it from leaving an area can potentially delay medical assistance.

In this case, according to the authorities and the medical workers’ account, the ambulance crew was able to escape and reach the hospital, but the driver sustained a serious injury in the process.

Romanian officials have once again called on the public to verify information before sharing it online, warning that manipulated images and AI-generated content can make false stories appear credible.

World.title: Did Hungary’s railway let you down? Here’s everything to know for a refund
World.content:
Summer travel in Hungary can bring more than sunshine and holidays. As temperatures rise, delays and disruptions on the country’s railway network can also become a familiar part of the journey.

Everything passengers need to know about ticket refunds, season tickets and compensation for railway delays

Whether the cause is extreme weather, the condition of railway infrastructure or rolling stock, an unexpected delay can quickly derail travel plans. A missed connection, cancelled programme or journey home that takes several hours longer than expected can also turn into a financial headache.

For passengers using Hungarian State Railways (Magyar Államvasutak, MÁV), however, several forms of reimbursement and compensation may be available. Crucially, they do not all apply in the same circumstances. Here is what passengers need to know in 2026 about MÁV ticket refunds, service-related refunds, delay compensation, season tickets and day tickets.

Ticket refund or compensation: what is the difference?

According to Pénzcentrum, when a train is delayed or cancelled, many passengers’ first thought is whether they can get their ticket money back. But Hungarian railway rules distinguish between several different situations. In practice, three cases are particularly important:

Voluntary ticket refund: when a passenger decides not to travel and returns their unused ticket before the journey.

Refund because of a railway service failure: when a delay, cancellation or other railway-related problem means the passenger cannot travel as originally planned.

Delay compensation: when the passenger completes the journey but arrives at their destination at least 20 minutes late.

The distinction matters because different procedures and compensation rules apply to each situation.

Returning a train ticket before departure

A standard ticket refund applies when a passenger decides not to use their ticket before starting the journey. This is not compensation for a delay; it is simply a decision not to travel. Timing is therefore crucial. For tickets bought at a railway ticket office or ticket machine, the refund can generally be requested at any station ticket office before the ticket’s validity begins.

Once the validity period has started, the refund can only be requested at the departure station, provided the passenger has not yet started their journey. For tickets purchased online or through the MÁV app, the refund must be initiated electronically before the ticket becomes valid.

The same deadline applies to Vármegye24 and Magyarország24 day tickets, as well as county and national season tickets: they must be returned before their validity begins. Passengers should also be aware that a voluntary refund does not necessarily mean receiving the entire purchase price. A handling fee may be deducted, depending on how and where the ticket was purchased.

How to return a MÁV ticket

The procedure depends on the method of purchase:

Ticket office: return the original paper ticket at a ticket office.

Ticket machine: the paper ticket must likewise be taken to a ticket office.

Online purchase by a registered user: select the relevant ticket from the previous purchases section of the MÁV online platform.

MÁV app: open the relevant ticket and select the refund option from its menu.

Online purchase without registration: the refund request must be submitted by email or telephone before the ticket becomes valid.

Once a ticket has been submitted for a refund, it can no longer be used for travel. For online purchases, the refunded amount is not paid in cash. Instead, it is returned to the bank account associated with the card used for the purchase.

What happens if the railway is at fault?

A different type of refund may apply when a passenger cannot make their planned journey because of a railway service failure. This could happen if a train is cancelled, delayed or otherwise disrupted for a reason attributable to the railway service.

This is different from voluntarily returning a ticket. In a service-related case, the passenger has not simply changed their mind about travelling; the railway disruption has prevented the journey from going ahead as planned. The distinction can also affect the amount refunded. While a voluntary refund may be subject to a handling fee, a refund resulting from a railway service failure may be made without such a deduction.

Passengers should obtain evidence of the disruption where possible. On a train, this can be requested from the ticket inspector; at a station, passengers can ask the staff member on duty. A delay certificate can also be requested through MÁV’s online system.

Once the necessary documentation has been obtained, passengers can submit their refund request through MÁV’s customer service channels or at a ticket office. Because service-related refunds may require central assessment, passengers should not necessarily expect the money to be returned immediately at the station.

Railway delay compensation in 2026: when does it apply?

The MÁV delay compensation scheme is designed for a different situation again: the passenger completes their journey, but their train arrives at the destination at least 20 minutes late. For domestic intercity and other eligible services, a delay of 20 minutes or more at the destination can trigger compensation.

For a single-journey ticket, this can mean a cash refund. For certain season tickets and day tickets, compensation takes the form of a credit that can be used towards a subsequent purchase.

Importantly, passengers cannot receive both a ticket refund and delay compensation for the same journey. If the fare has already been refunded, the same journey cannot also generate compensation under the delay scheme.

Single-journey tickets: 50 per cent back after a 20-minute delay

For an eligible single-journey ticket, a train arriving at least 20 minutes late can entitle the passenger to 50 per cent of the ticket price under the delay compensation scheme. The passenger must have actually made the journey, and the ticket price must not already have been refunded.

For tickets purchased online or through the MÁV app, the compensation is processed automatically. Passengers can check the relevant information in the Previous purchases section of the online platform or app.

Tickets purchased at a ticket office, from a machine or on board require a separate claim. In these cases, passengers can submit their delay compensation request through MÁV’s online system, either as a registered user or as a guest. The ticket details and payment information required to process the compensation must be provided.

What about MÁV season tickets and day tickets?

Season tickets and day tickets work somewhat differently. For county and national season tickets, as well as Vármegye24 and Magyarország24 day tickets, eligible delays can result in a 10 per cent credit towards the purchase of another product of the same type.

This is therefore not normally a cash payment into the passenger’s bank account. Instead, it functions as a credit or voucher for a future purchase. The number of qualifying delays required depends on the type of ticket.

Vármegye24 and Magyarország24 day tickets

A single delay of at least 20 minutes during the validity of the day ticket can qualify the passenger for compensation. The credit is equivalent to 10 per cent of the price of the day ticket and can be used towards the purchase of another day ticket of the same type.

County and national season tickets

For a county season ticket or national season ticket, passengers generally need to accumulate at least five delays of 20 minutes or more during the ticket’s validity period. Once the threshold has been reached, the passenger can receive a credit equivalent to 10 per cent of the price of the relevant season ticket.

How is delay compensation recorded?

The process depends on whether the passenger uses a digital or paper ticket. For digital season tickets and day tickets, passengers should select the service they actually travelled on in the MÁV+ app. If that service arrives at least 20 minutes late, the delay can be recorded against the ticket.

Once the required number of qualifying delays has been accumulated, an electronic voucher is issued. This can then be used when purchasing another product of the same type. Passengers travelling with paper season tickets or day tickets cannot rely on the app to record their delays.

Instead, they should request a delay certificate for every qualifying journey and keep the original season ticket or day ticket. The relevant credit can subsequently be claimed when purchasing another product of the same type at a ticket office, with the certificates presented as evidence.

More on the country’s railway network: Hungary reopens railway line closed 3 years ago – videos, photos

Lump-sum compensation for delayed trains

There is another form of compensation that passengers may be entitled to in certain circumstances: lump-sum compensation. This applies to eligible domestic trains that require a supplement or seat reservation, provided the passenger has a valid ticket and reservation. The amount depends on the length of the delay:

30–119 minutes: 25 per cent of the relevant fare.

120 minutes or more: 50 per cent.

If the calculated compensation is HUF 1,000 or less, it is not paid out on its own. However, several smaller claims can be combined.

For tickets bought at a ticket office or ticket machine, passengers can claim lump-sum compensation at any station ticket office within 14 days. For electronic tickets, or where the 14-day period for making the claim at a ticket office has passed, passengers should submit their claim through MÁV’s customer service channels.

The claim requires sufficient information to identify the ticket. For electronic tickets, passengers may need to provide the PDF ticket or purchase details. Bank account or postal details may also be required for payment.

What should passengers do when a train is delayed?

The most important thing is not to treat every disruption as a simple ticket refund. Before making a claim, passengers should establish which situation applies:

Did you decide not to travel before departure? This is a voluntary ticket refund. Could you not travel because of a railway-related disruption? You may be entitled to a service-related refund. Did you complete your journey but arrive at least 20 minutes late? Delay compensation may apply.

Passengers should also obtain and retain any relevant documentation as soon as possible. This is particularly important for paper tickets and season tickets, where delay certificates may be needed to support a later claim.

For digital tickets and passes, using the appropriate MÁV app functions can make the process considerably easier, as eligible delays can be recorded electronically. With several different compensation mechanisms now available, knowing which one applies can make the difference between successfully recovering money or missing out on compensation after a disrupted journey.

World.title: Viktor Orbán filmed in Serbia with MOL executive and controversial Hatvanpuszta estate architect
World.content:
Former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán was spotted at a popular trumpet festival in Serbia, where he was filmed walking through the streets alongside two figures with close links to Hungarian business and the controversial Hatvanpuszta estate.

Former Hungarian prime minister photographed at Guča festival with two prominent associates

Orbán’s appearance at the Guča Trumpet Festival in the Dragačevo region was reported by Serbian news agency RINA, which published footage showing the former prime minister mingling with festival-goers and posing for photographs.

According to RINA, the former prime minister appeared to be in good spirits and was walking without bodyguards while enjoying the festival in the company of friends. However, the identities of the two men walking alongside him have attracted particular attention.

MOL executive and businessman among Orbán’s companions

One of the men accompanying Orbán was identified as Oszkár Világi, a Slovak-Hungarian billionaire and deputy chief executive officer of Hungarian oil and gas company MOL. Világi is the former head of Slovnaft, the Slovak refinery owned by MOL, and is also the majority owner of Slovak football club FK DAC 1904, based in Dunajská Streda.

Investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi also identified Világi in the footage, noting his longstanding relationship with Orbán. The two have maintained close ties for years, according to Panyi’s account. Világi’s appearance alongside Orbán is notable in part because the two remained connected despite Hungary’s recent political changes, according to the reporting.

Hatvanpuszta architect also seen in the footage

The other man walking with Orbán was identified as architect Dániel Taraczky. Taraczky has been associated with the development of the Orbán family’s Hatvanpuszta estate, a property that has attracted considerable political and public attention in Hungary.

According to official documents cited in the Hungarian reports, Taraczky acted as an architect representing Orbán’s father, Győző Orbán, during heritage-protection proceedings concerning the estate. He has also reportedly won public procurement contracts connected to a number of construction projects financed with public funds.

The Hatvanpuszta luxury estate. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

Never miss a headline: join our newly-launched Messenger group!

Disciplinary proceedings over Hatvanpuszta building

Taraczky’s role at Hatvanpuszta has previously drawn criticism from independent MP Ákos Hadházy. Hadházy filed a complaint with the Hungarian Chamber of Architects over the demolition of a protected 19th-century agricultural building at the estate.

In May 2026, the chamber’s ethics and disciplinary committee ruled at first instance that Taraczky had breached legal requirements and professional ethical rules. The committee suspended his chamber membership for one year and imposed a fine of HUF 800,000 (appr. EUR 2,190), as well as ordering him to pay procedural costs. The ruling was a first-instance disciplinary decision, according to the reports.

A relaxed appearance at one of Serbia’s best-known festivals

The footage from Guča presents an informal picture of Orbán, who is shown walking among festival-goers and stopping to take photographs with members of the public. The Guča Trumpet Festival is one of Serbia’s best-known traditional music events, attracting large crowds to the small town in western Serbia each year.

While Orbán’s presence at the festival itself was relatively informal, the appearance of Világi and Taraczky alongside him has drawn attention to the former prime minister’s relationships with prominent business figures and people connected to projects associated with his family.
